Notes: This volume is number 32 in the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies (K.S.T.S. series; however, it was erroneously printed as volume 31 on both the English and Sanskrit title pages. In one specimen examined, the volume number had been manually altered—likely by the printers or publishers—to the correct number (32), whereas in another specimen examined, it had not been corrected. This volume is mistakenly listed as volume 31 in many (though not all) library and bibliographic records consulted, including the *Descriptive Analysis of the Kashmir Series of Texts & Studies*; nevertheless, the first volume of the *Svacchanda Tantra* is invariably and correctly titled as volume 31 of the K.S.T.S. series.

Volume Number 31:
The Śrīmālinīvijayavārtika,
composed by the venerable Mahāmāheśvara Ācārya Abhinavaguptapāda.
In the Pratividyāprakāśa (Research) Institute established by His Majesty Śrī Pratāpasiṃha, the Great King of Kaśmīra and the Sun of Dharma for Śrī Bhārata.

This was compiled by the Superintendent, Paṇḍita Madhusūdana Kaula Śāstrī, with the assistance of other scholars at the designated office, following its collection, critical editing, pagination, and the addition of explanatory notes and indices.

It has been printed and brought to publication at the Pratāpa Steam Press in Śrīnagara, Kashmir, after being prepared with an introduction in a modern, accessible, and pure style approved by Western scholarly circles.

Now follows the *Śrīmālinīvijayavārttika*, which has been brought under [the author's] own control by the most excellent of the great kings who have spoken it.
The First Section, composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta:
[Salutation to] the Great Mother, who is the source of ever-new creation resting upon the stainless creative power (*kalā*).

May my heart— the lineage of the nectar of the Absolute (anuttara), consisting of the emission of the state that flashes forth from the union of those two [Father and Mother], whose body is full and whose splendor is concealed by five faces— throb with radiance! 1.
May that Guru be victorious, by whose radiant rays of awakening our lotus-hearts have blossomed on every side. (2)

To me, he has granted floods of wealth—blazing with the six objects of touch, the three objects of taste, and the five streams of sensory experience—which are dedicated to the vow of crushing poverty. (3)
May Śambhunātha, who is gracious toward the virtuous devotees purified by auspicious wisdom, be pleased with me, gratified by the flower of my speech. (4)
I pay homage to the one named Śrī Cukhala, who is more venerable even than my gurus; refined by his grace, I now abide with all worldly attachments dissolved. (5)
May the illustrious Bhūtirāja, the great-minded one who is even more venerable than that, and whose daring consists in uplifting the multitude of his devotees, be victorious! (6)
Victorious are these compositions, which diffuse the fragrance of consciousness and spread in all directions, originating from the awakening of Śrī Somānanda and the illustrious Utpala. 7.
Victorious is the word of the venerable teacher Lakṣmaṇagupta, who teaches the recognition (pratyabhijñā) that cuts through the cycle of existence born of that [dualistic] vision. ||8||
By this [work], my intellect-bee, intoxicated solely by the wonder of tasting the flavor of countless new [verses], has been satiated with the supreme enjoyment. (9)
Having attained a state of oneness with that, she remains thus within her own self;
therefore, various riches of sound (nāda) manifest from her. 10.
Requested again and again by the ears of my true disciple, I shall explain the meaning of the words wherever they occur in the venerable *Mālinī*. (11)

Because it proceeds through propriety by avoiding what is inappropriate between the signified and the signifier, this work is rightly called a *vārtika*, a treatise that both turns [toward] and turns away from [the subject]. 12.
I bow to those Abhinavaguptas, who shine day and night yet remain beyond the reach of all, and who are like a mass of rays from the moon of Śiva. 13.
Victorious are the rays of the moon of knowledge arising from the mouth of the Supreme Lord, capable of destroying the adversaries of the world's bliss! (14)
Because its true being is unrestrained and it partakes solely in the non-difference of all entities,
that great primordial knowledge which arose previously is the Bhairava of the mass of rays.

Then, that [reality], which is devoid of such things to be rejected or accepted as belong to one's own māyā, is distinguished solely by the variegated state of the rays of its expanded manifestation. ||16||
That heart of the Supreme Lord has the nature of touch;
therein, too, the Great Lord is eternally present through His power, which is identical with His own self.
When, having encountered union, one attains the supreme meditative absorption, then his supreme face becomes the locus for the expansion of emission (visarga). ||18||
That which exists as the seed of all, beautiful with the bliss of the world arising from unsurpassed expansion, and indistinguishable from the future face [of the Lord]. (19)
That [state] is considered to be the heart-beat, the gaze, the supreme essence, the nameless, the waveless, and so forth;
this is the supreme Trika, previously described as subtle (*sūkṣma*), which possesses the non-differentiation of all powers.
Herein occurs the falling away from the contraction of doubt regarding the manifestation of objective existence.
This triad of will, action, and vision consists solely of the state of being absorbed in one's own bliss.
And likewise, the Gurus have described it thus in the *Śaivadarśana*:

"As long as the state of transmigratory existence—which consists of the delusion characterized by the non-recognition of identity with Śiva—has not yet dawned, even during that time, Śiva-nature exists in the form already described; and likewise, at that moment, the fivefold power (*śaktipañcaka*), though of a single nature, [remains so]."

From the perspective of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), because the effect is possible, [the Self] indeed exists. For instance, that very light which consists of the innate reflective awareness "I am" throughout successive states—being independent of anything else due to its fullness—is established as being of the nature of bliss and composed of pure consciousness; that itself is primary autonomy.

Śivatā has been described as "the delight of consciousness" (cidāhlāda). Experience and manifestation occur solely within the fullness of conscious bliss, not in the external world; therefore, that in which [all else] dissolves into that very state is thus defined, and by this, the consciousness of one who has attained fulfillment (nirvṛtacit) is expressed.
However, will, knowledge, and action become manifest only in relation to distinct objects and so forth. In the supreme state (parāvasthā),...

Furthermore, as long as one's own nature shines forth as "I am full," that very [nature] is knowledge because it is luminosity; that same [nature] is action because it consists of impetus (*saṃrambha*); and since its acceptance is due to having that as its inherent nature, will (*icchā*) is also established therein. Thus he says: "Will is just that much," and that much is the essential nature (*svarūpa*).

The word "action" (*kriyā*) is to be supplied [to complete the sense]. Alternatively, in the phrase "firstly, knowledge" (*atha vā tāvajjñānam*), the word *tāvat* is to be transformed into the feminine gender to agree with "action";
however, the second occurrence of *tāvat* at the end has the sense of sequence, referring to the various states such as the supreme (*parā*) and non-supreme (*aparā*). For this very reason:

Even in the absence of distinct objects, because the acceptance [of the object], its manifestation, and the exertion [toward it] are always of the nature of light and do not waver, they possess the very fitness for the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) of will and so forth; this has been stated as "extremely subtle" (*susūkṣma*).
It is "extremely subtle" because, due to the absence of things such as the desired object, no conceptual differentiation (*vibhāga*) is imagined. For this very reason...

The state of equilibrium with Śakti has been described as having the nature of the manifestation of pure consciousness alone, and as being supremely the delight of consciousness; that very same undivided supreme state is called "the Beyond" (para) when it abides in this manner. When he abides thus, merged in the experience of the mere delight of consciousness... [ŚDV 4] ...he remains absorbed in that. 22.
To that extent is His will, to that extent is His knowledge, and indeed to that extent is His action;
He exists in the state of equilibrium among the three extremely subtle powers.
"Then, being non-different from that supreme delight of the nature of consciousness, one should become [that].
But surely, in such a state which is the soul of the universe, because of the absence of contraction... (24)
How can the excellence of the scriptures and so forth have their root in conceptual construction?
It is said: this entire cognition consists of the radiance of pure consciousness. (25)
Because it is conjoined with the nature of luminosity, its essence consists of the dense mass of the awareness of consciousness (cid-āmarśa).
In that regard, this very light which shines forth has the nature of awareness (āmarśa-svabhāva). ||26||
Why is this very flood of scriptures not sufficient; what is the use of other displays of logic?
In that regard, he would merely be pierced by the goddess of speech belonging to others. (27)
But it is not variegated by a collection of colors belonging to worldly illusion.

[Here the commentary states: For the Lord, whose nature is consciousness, there is a manifestation of objects as non-different from Himself, just as there is within His own self; otherwise, reflective awareness—which consists in being the creator—would have only the appearing object as its domain.

It would not have the form of a voluntary act. [Pratyabhijñā-hṛdaya 1.5.10] It has been stated in the venerable *Pratyabhijñā* that there is the manifestation of that which resides within the Self. (18)
Indeed, without that [reflective awareness], desire does not proceed;
otherwise, they know reflective awareness to be the very nature of manifestation. (29)

"Even though light is colored by objects, it is equal to gems and the like" [here the commentary states: "The primary nature of light is self-reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*); without that, this [light], despite having forms differentiated by objects, possesses only transparency and not non-inertness, because of the absence of wonder (*camatkṛti*)"].
Furthermore, whatever name exists here is within the sphere of the wonder of consciousness.

At that time, this [consciousness] becomes manifest with respect to objects such as those named "delight" and so forth, by virtue of its surging upward while taking the internal reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of those [objects] as its support. //31//
And later it becomes perfectly clear, as the Guru has said:
"Just as pleasure and so forth, established by one's own consciousness, remain [as such]. (32)
For at the time of its own establishment, it is not experienced by its own self-awareness;
thus it must necessarily be accepted as such, because of the proof provided by self-awareness. ||33||

In the same way, here too, on the path of the unfolding of subsequent knowledge and so forth, one should continue to contemplate until that ground which consists entirely of non-duality is reached. (34)
To that extent, by virtue of the clarity of a portion of the sublime discernment appropriate to it,
that very [text] attains the status of a scripture (*śāstra*) through its prior emission. (35)
But this alone would be appropriate, for even in the case of the supreme state beyond all substrates (anupadhi), some trace of the practice of the scriptural meaning is still perceived. (36)
He is indeed possessed of the powers of primordial consciousness and the rest, which constitute the very essence of manifestation;
through the influence of limiting adjuncts, he is further augmented by their respective diversities.
Just as the manifestation of a face occurs in water, a mirror, a gem, or a sword, so too does its state appear as flickering, upright, circular, subtle, long, and so forth. (38)
Thus, in this supreme form, the riches of knowledge have arisen, beautiful with the threefold nature of the seed of the heart that is uninterrupted. (39)
But when Bhairava, empowered by his own energy (śakti), desires to emit the flood of objective states—which consist of various internal waves of shifting forms—[then the universe unfolds]. (40)
Then those very perfections of consciousness, born of that limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), seemed as if they had resorted to the constraint of performing even slight ritual actions. (41)
Even though it has assumed the nature of a flood of waves all around,
nevertheless, in the Bhairava of consciousness, which is beautiful with the bliss of the world— 42.
When the powerful one is satisfied by the mere fullness of his own being,
and when the state of being a possessor of power (the subject) is eclipsed by his own perfect power (the object), [then he is truly worshipped].
In that very same way, the stream of consciousness, whose essence is reflective awareness, unfolds;
within it, a certain delight arises through the instruction on enjoyment. (44)
For the fortunate ones, even the multitude of enjoyments—when cultivated through confidence in their consciousness, conduct, and practice—leads to the state of supreme liberation. (45)

It is said therein that the Lord’s fondness for sacrifice, which is filled with the intensity of the agitation of His own powers and so forth, is especially directed toward the midst of the Mothers. (46)
Through the surging power of sovereignty, having attained the designation of the state of Īśvara, this God, whose majesty is supreme knowledge, has arisen and been fully manifested. 47.

In this case as well, through the conjunction and disjunction of infinite constituent parts, and by means of the synthesis of the distinctions between prior states, an incalculability is attained. (48)
It is solely through the power of those limiting adjuncts that the various manifestations of the scriptures, rituals, and knowledge— which are devoid of the state of pure consciousness— are extended.

This primary manifestation (prapañca), however, is analyzed as having a fivefold nature. And so it will be stated: "The waking state, characterized primarily by the power of action (kriyā-śakti) due to Śiva’s active engagement, consists—by virtue of His sovereignty and through His own freedom—of various unique creations characterized primarily by the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti)."

Dreaming consists primarily of will (*icchā*), acting as an impeller characterized by the departure from indifference through the absence of knowledge and action; deep sleep consists primarily of the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*) through the cessation of that [will] due to the fullness of the object of desire; and the fourth state (*turya*) consists primarily of the absence of bliss.

The meaning is that, because it rests in its own essential nature which is all-encompassing and complete, the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*)—which is characterized primarily by the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*)—consists of five states; thus, although reality (*tattva*) is non-different, it is fivefold. [50]

"Because [the Self] possesses activity and sovereignty, because it impels that which is dependent on it, because desire ceases, and because of its purity"—by such collections of statements as these. (51)
Indeed, within such a vast expanse, distinctions created by space, time, and form do not exist at all; we say "certainly, so be it. 52.
For here not even the mere name of the reality of time is perceived;
even the all-pervasive power of Mahākālī does not manifest here. (53)

In that case, when it is undivided and self-sufficient, what indeed is the purpose of adopting this verbal formulation: "then later again," and "from another" (where the reading is *parataścaitikonmeṣa*)? 54.

To this we reply: it is indeed true that, in reality, even when the creation of the principles has unfolded within the manifest Self, and even when Time itself has opened its eyes [the reading "kālo'pi" is preferred]. ||55||
For consciousness, these conceptual constructions of "prior" and "subsequent" do not exist at all,
because time functions as a differentiator only by way of being a qualifying attribute.
And that is called a qualifier when it is expressed by way of coordination, such that it becomes cognized as distinct [from the qualified], as in the case of "the blue lotus. (57)
And the state of being an object of cognition for consciousness is never logically possible;
for the state of being an object of cognition is the state of appearing, which occurs through the grace of its own illumination. (58)
If that light were conscious because it resides within another consciousness,
then, due to the lack of restriction regarding lights, an infinite regress (anavasthā) would certainly ensue.
Therefore, those who, being utterly deluded, claim that awakening—which is essentially the manifestation of objects—is itself unmanifest, are indeed deceived by their own words. (60)
Therefore, time is not capable of creating a distinction within consciousness; nor is this time able to act as a differentiator of the object of knowledge. 61.
For the universe is non-different from consciousness; if it were otherwise, it would not appear.
An object appears as variegated when it is permeated by light. 62.
In this way, the universal illumination (viśvaprakāśa) would be eternal for everyone;
for when that which is called "awakening" (bodha) exists as illumination, it attains the state of being illumination itself.
If even a non-luminous entity were perceived as having the nature of luminosity, then the fact that this entity is indeed non-luminous would have darkness alone as its refuge. (64)
And if that which is non-luminous by nature were made luminous,
then surely that entity would be destroyed, because it has fallen away from its own state of non-luminosity (or, according to another reading, its own state of self-luminosity). [65]
Even the Creator is not capable of making that which is not of such a nature manifest;
for indeed, this state of "this-ness" appears only when there is manifestation.
Let this very thing be so; however, let that which is unmanifest shine forth in this manner.
And when the unmanifest nature of an entity has been made manifest, [the following occurs].
It would not be the case that the state of things is such that an entity is manifested in this way;
therefore, enough with this separate manifestation—Śiva is thus [self-luminous].
Therefore, that which is sung as the supreme Śiva is indeed this very Light;
it possesses inconceivable majesty and is whirled about by the unrestrained power of its own freedom.
In that same way, the state of the Immutable shines forth through those various natures;
here, no one at all suspects the existence of any omniscient being anywhere.
"I, Caitra, know the jar, but I do not know the cloth; both of them I know.
This cloth does not know it, but I, that very person, know both the jar and the cloth. (71)
I shall know it, or not; previously I did not know it at all, nor do I know it anywhere.
I know it successively, or simultaneously, or by both, or devoid of both.
I know everything, yet I know nothing at all; I am not anyone whatsoever.
Indeed, I am not the nature of objective existence; I am always both the "I" and the "all. (73)
"I alone am everything; what else could all this be?"—in such ways, this single Light alone unfolds itself. (74)
If this one [light] is indeed some kind of illumination, then how could another not exist?
Oh, how deluded you are! How can such a person be instructed? //75//
A single light shines in manifold forms due to its autonomy;
yet in reality, it is neither manifold nor non-manifold, because of the defects inherent in the notion of difference. (76)
If the manifestation of a cloth were possible within the manifestation of a jar, that would not be the manifestation of the jar; for it would then be a dual manifestation. ||77||
That [light] indeed exists for us; it is not non-existent as you have urged.
It remains established such that there may be no manifestation of this [object] in the form of a jar. (78)
And that is illogical; since manifestation is consciousness, its definition is simply the unfolding of its own self.
If that is so, what is the point of this vain display of verbal proliferation? (79)
The characteristic of the insentient is indeed its limited luminosity; for consciousness, being distinct from the insentient, is not so delimited. (80)
Therefore, since the existence of the sun is established, what fool indeed would say:
"How is it that this [sun] fills the entire earth with its own rays? (81)
Therefore, since this Light is established, whatever conceptualizations there may be regarding that Light are like the observance of a woman’s conduct by one who has enjoyed her with everyone. 82.
And if manifestation is unestablished, who am I, what are you, and what even is darkness?
Or what could there be that is nothing at all; or how indeed could there even be silence? (83)
Therefore, for even those entities that have attained the state of Bhairava through identity with the Light, this time is incapable of doing anything at all. (84)
Well then, how is it that the sequence of words beginning with "tadā" [occurs]?
Listen; although this has already been stated, it is being explained again by way of analysis. (85)
That which is light appears in this very way, manifesting as such and such;
it does not belong to anyone else at all, yet it shines forth in its own right. //86//
He alone is supremely noble and the illuminator of all;
he is autonomous, and thus his will is power—[the reading is *śaktisvātantrya*]—designated as autonomy. 87.
And that [consciousness], resting within itself due to the absence of anything other than it, is this very rest in its own self which is called the bliss of the Lord. (88)
Or rather, the majesty of His sovereignty exists as non-distinct from His own essential nature; within His own self-luminous abode, He causes the delusions of objective phenomena to appear. 89.

And it is stated in the scriptures that manifestation is the power of action (kriyā-śakti), by which the differentiation of the various categories of reality (tattva) and so forth is brought about. (90)
And how indeed could manifestation be conceived if it were not manifest?
Therefore, that manifestation residing within this [consciousness] is known as my power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti). ||81||
This much is the form of this God as consisting solely of his own self; that is declared to be his "unmesha" (expansion), from which the all-pervasive Lord [emerges] with five powers. ||92||
Whether the deity exists as three powers or as a single power, or as the deity alone;
or whether that goddess is indeed Śakti herself—she is thus described in the scripture. (93)
And it will be stated by the Great Lord [Śiva] later on, beginning with the words "The world-element has been described," that she, though one, indeed attains manifoldness. (94)
And this very [reality], well-established in its own self through repose in intense bliss, is expressed by its congenial formulations of words, such as "Bhairava" and so forth. (95)
Whether it be near or far away, whatever collection of sounds may exist for him, or even anything else belonging to the Lord, does not exist in reality. //96//
And so this Lord indeed manifests in such and such ways;
therefore, this entire sequence of conceptual construction follows accordingly. (97)
Nor is that merely a mental construction; even if it were so, what loss would there be?
Whether the Lord intends it thus, or whether He constructs it thus—this Self of Light remains beyond the thirty-sevenfold nature.
Manifesting a variety of appearances, the Lord causes time to appear. ||99||
This very manifestation of variety is declared to be the power of time;
therefore, in accordance with this manifesting power of time, [the following occurs]. (100)
From our own [position], the subsequent coloring (uparāga) proceeds in that manner;
yet it is not the case that this [coloring] does not exist there at all—for how could that which does not exist there [be produced]? ||101||
Otherwise, that which is called "transformation" (tanyatā) would be subject to its own manifestation;
but surely, this being so, it applies to other networks of principles (tattva-jāla) as well, regarding their state as either pure or impure. (102)
Whether in the pure or impure state, or in the circle of principles (tattva-maṇḍala) such as the Vidyā and others,
there will be no distinction because of the true existence of Śuddhabhairava.
Alas, we dance about; indeed, we must explain that which revolves of its own accord within the heart of your long-lived self. (104)
Indeed, the distinction between the pure and the impure does not exist in discourses on the ultimate truth; yet that very distinction remains fixed in the minds of the deluded. (105)
If the distinction known as "pure" and "impure" is not real, then this very scripture intended for exposition would be in contradiction [with itself]. (106)
"For there is impurity of the principles, and their purification occurs through initiation";
since such is the state here, which is manifoldly dominated by duality. (107)
It is said: in this non-dual reality, duality does not exist at all in any way;
for it has been stated that even in the all-pervading Lord, who is devoid of differentiation, there is the appearance of differentiation. (108)

Indeed, that very state is called "saṃsāra" by such terms as "māyā," "avidyā," and so forth; it is also termed "bandha" (bondage)—the reading "gandha" is found in some manuscripts—and those who are immersed therein are considered "saṃsārin" (transmigrating beings).
The determination of their purity, impurity, and so forth, follows from reflecting upon that;
moreover, this scripture correctly teaches the yoga of the Blessed One. (110)
They declare the yoga of the Blessed One to be non-dual and free from the pairs of opposites;
its instruction would be thus only if it were characterized by differentiation. (111)
That [duality] is conceived through devotion to Him, yet it is defined as being utterly severed;
for in the case of entering and resting within the all-pervading Lord Advaita-Bhairava, [such duality is absent]. 112.
There is no state resulting from practice, for those two [doubt and certainty] have difference as their sole lifeblood;
therefore, for the removal of all possible suspicions regarding duality— //113//
Effort is exerted by all toward both teachers and pupils;
therefore, having raised every doubt regarding duality here, everything is set forth. (114)
Therefore, having considered all possible courses of action, one should not remain indifferent even toward that [ultimate goal].
For if duality has not been wiped away, then reality is indeed only one. (115)
That Brahman is Consciousness alone; therefore, enough with the determination of enumerations of principles.
Why is the number of principles defined as twenty-five? (116)
Therefore, as long as one perceives the movement of duality—which exists as the nature of differentiation—one should effect its rejection; by that, freedom from doubt shall arise. (117)
And this very instruction is given by piercing through consciousness itself;
it is the tearing asunder of those wings of the vajra that correspond to its possible manifestations. //118//
For thus it has been said by the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa in his *Śrīstotra*:
"Homage to you, who, having brought forth the delusion of those bewildered by worldly existence, shatters that very delusion. (119)
And having chosen knowledge-bliss (jñānānanda), which is free from dualities, O Lord, they reveal it.

[O Lord of independent action, those who are bewildered in this world of transmigration (bhava) due to being deluded by the power of Your Māyā, and because of their attachment to duality, are devoted to ritual action (karmaniṣṭha); for them, in the first stage—]
Having manifested each respective delusion of duality, they shatter it within the sphere of the final doctrine (*siddhānta*) for the sake of its destruction;
likewise, having embraced the supreme non-dual form of knowledge-bliss (*jñānānanda*), which consists of consciousness-bliss (*vijñānamānandamaya*),
they first conceal it from the unqualified because of its secret nature, and subsequently reveal it to those who are qualified.

Homage to you who make [this] clear! And thus, that very nature of the *karmakāṇḍa* which was shown by the Blessed One as something to be abandoned (*heyatvena*) because it constitutes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*),
is accepted by the deluded as something to be adopted (*upādeyatvena*), and they claim that the *jñānakāṇḍa* is merely a corroborative statement (*arthavāda*).

Alternatively, it was by the Blessed One himself, for the sake of protecting the fourfold duties such as creation, that those [beings] were established in such a state, being both consoled and deluded. (Sta0 Ci0 71, śloka)
"Free from duality" means that the non-dual state is made manifest. ||120||
And the word "ca" (and) here is intended to bring about wonder, signifying that "errors are also manifested";
furthermore, it will be elaborated upon later that in this system, non-duality alone is the truth.

It will be stated later that the purification of the paths and so forth are untenable in a state of duality; yet, if this is not possible without non-duality, why should it not be possible even without duality? (122)
This is true; however, it is not the case that a distinction between the two principles is untenable.
For this is indeed that supreme non-duality (*parādvaita*) in which there is neither the abandonment nor the grasping of difference. (123)
Since all things exist as distinct through their own respective natures, I consider this word "non-difference" to actually differentiate aesthetic flavors. 124.
Therefore, enough with this; let that which is relevant be examined:
how indeed the Supreme Lord manifests the conceptualization of duality.
Surely time also unfolds in that same manner. ||125||
Nevertheless, he never at any time undergoes differentiation from the perspective of ultimate reality;
for he is simultaneously of the nature of pure consciousness.
By virtue of its autonomy, it manifests in manifold ways. ||126||
They employ this term "simultaneous" (yugapat) with the intention of excluding succession and time; for indeed, in this [state] whose essence is the reflective awareness of a single, compact being—
Whatever variegated action I perform in consciousness, or whatever I know, others such as Maitra or Caitra cannot do that; or else, why would they not know it? (127)
Oh, how exceedingly dense is this knot of illusion!
For we declare here that there is not even a single thing called "self" or "other" in this world;
the notion "I know" is merely the manifestation of a particular form, such as a jar or a body.
It has been stated that diverse forms shine within the supreme light. ||128||
Therefore, in the cognition "I know the jar," there is indeed no difference whatsoever; for it appears to me that "this is a jar. Thus, the manifestation of difference exists.
