This very [cognition] has its form rendered turbid by contact with mud. (301)
One who desires to bathe runs toward the waters of a mirage in the desert;
if it were possible for a single entity to exist despite having distinct natures and so forth, [then such a thing might occur]. (302)

In that case, the difference [between things] due to a difference in their causes is not ultimately real. Or, if it is maintained that [an entity] has a differentiated nature and yet is one; || 303 ||
If it is argued that "a difference in intrinsic nature leads to [a difference in] the effect," then this vow would have to be abandoned.
But surely, in this way, let that action not be one; rather, let wood and other such factors be the causal agents.
Let it be so even for those things that produce an effect; for we have no objection, since what we call "action" is nothing other than this very power. (305)
And power (śakti), through the postulation of its differentiation from the fruit, is essentially the existent itself in its various aspects;
that power belongs only to the All-pervasive One (Vibhu), and He is the embodiment of the universal self.
In ultimate reality, it is not divided by the distinction between the result and the agent;
for although the omnipresent [Self] is non-dual within its own nature, it thus manifests as differentiated. (307)
That by which the Great Lord is the agent is called the power of action (kriyā-śakti).
But how can that which bound souls (paśus) perform be logically established? ||308||
For they, because their very life consists of differentiation, would perform actions characterized by differentiation.
Enough of this; how could the bound souls (paśus) possibly act clearly [in such a way]? 309.
That very argument is cut off by its own words, like the son of a barren woman;
for the potter can never, at any time or place, possess the status of a creator [of himself]. (310)
If that [effect] does not partake of non-difference from a creator who is called "Great," then why is it that a cloth is not also produced by a potter? (311)
Now, is it not the case that even a jar is made by a potter? If so, why should the Lord lack agency over a cloth as well, given His status as the creator of the universe? (312)
If this were so, there would be no other agent of actions; toward whom, then, would the causality of auspicious and inauspicious deeds exist in order to produce their own fruit? (313)
It is just so, O Venerable One; for those who understand it thus, there is no fruit whatsoever arising from the auspicious or the inauspicious anywhere. (314)
Thus, those who do not know this eat as the unwise;
that very thing, known by the name *karman* (or *kārmam*, according to another reading), is impurity rooted in ignorance.
Accepting this very point—that it is mere consciousness alone—some indeed maintain that [the self] is a non-agent, because agency is logically untenable. (316)

For that which is said to be its agency, being in excess of its nature as consciousness, would impart insentience to it, because of the consequence that consciousness would then be the predominant factor.
"Surely the agency of primordial nature (prakṛti) is metaphorically attributed to the person (puruṣa);
this is merely prattled about in vain within the home by those who have strayed from the path of logic. (318)
For metaphorical designation does not establish the actual reality of things;
let there be such a designation, provided it remains devoid of a corresponding real entity. (319)
Even when designated by the figurative term "fire," a man does not remove the cold produced by snowdrifts, spray, rain, or wind. (320)
Prakṛti is not proclaimed to be the seer of the Puruṣa,
nor is there any other wretched being besides them who could metaphorically possess the status of an agent;
furthermore, what purpose would there be for such a person in the conventional usage of agency?
But a designation is not capable of transforming a non-existent thing. ||322||
Even those logicians who have arrived at the conclusion that the self is the agent must first address this question presented to our intellect. (323)
How can that agency which is established in the world through the performance of action, and which consists of movement, be possible in the All-pervasive One who is devoid of movement? (324)
Now, it may be objected: "Knowledge, the desire to act, and effort—these three qualities inhere [in the soul]; why then is its status as an object (karmatva) cited in this context? ||325||
In this way, the intellects of those with childish minds may be deceived by impostors;
even children would not know [anything] devoid of cognition. (326)
In that regard, knowledge is not the agent; for it exists everywhere. Likewise, desire and effort also generally reside in everyone, in every respect. (327)
What could a potter, whose mind is tormented by the absence of a home, do for himself—even though he knows what is needed, desires it, and exerts effort—if he does not possess a house? (328)
Surely he does not know how to build; therefore he does not desire to build;
and because of that, he does not exert himself to build—how then can he have that house built?

If the very form "to act" (kartum) is indeed a qualifier of knowledge and the other [faculties], then what would be the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do) therein, if it were indeed characterized by vibration (*saspaṇdatā*)? 330.
Then one might say that he "knows how to move" or "desires to move";
yet that movement belongs to his own self, for it arises from the manifestation of his sovereign power.
Furthermore, a non-vibrating cognition may arise for anyone;
and the possession of cognition, desire, and effort is stated to be its instrument. (332)
Regarding the phrase "to act for oneself," when its meaning is thus analyzed:
one knows, desires, exerts effort, strives to know, strives to exert effort, and strives to desire. (333)
The meaning of "each one" is expressed by the word "he knows how to act";
this would be the state of desiring to act (*cikīrṣitṛtva*), but it would not be actual agency (*kartṛtva*). || 334 ||
If that were the case, verbal and physical actions would become identical to mental ones;
or else, how could agency belong to this [person] through verbal and physical actions? (335)
How can it be said that even mental actions belong to him, given the presence of those three qualities [of the self] which give rise to actions of mind, speech, and body? (336)

If it is argued that this [self] is a partaker of karma because of the accumulation of karmas, then surely this would be a mere metaphorical designation (upacāra); and it has already been explained that such a designation refers to something that is not a real entity.

Furthermore, when other substances such as the self, magnitude, and so forth, along with their qualities, are present, would that [self] also become the locus of agency simply because those [qualities] exist? (338)
Nor should it be accepted that this [defect] exists even in liberation (mukti)—for indeed, it would exist there as well;
since this same rule applies equally when other qualities of the self are present. (339)

[If it were so,] actions would proceed from themselves, resulting in the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done. Furthermore, [this would apply] everywhere where dependence on an intelligent being is required, even in the case of God. (340)

If causality were attributed to an effect that exceeds its [constituent] arrangement, when it has already been filled by its own respective parts of inherence and other causes, [then causality would be redundant]. (341)
Granted that the potter and others may possess causality with respect to their own respective portions;
however, there is not even a trace of a portion for which [the Lord] would be the cause in relation to the Universal Creator. (342)
There is no agency other than knowledge, desire, and effort;
therefore, agency could never belong to anything else. (343)
They know that even for the Lord of Lords, sovereignty is his agency;
thus, it is the same for the Supreme Lords, whether their selves are in a state of difference or non-difference. (344)
Actions do not have the inherent power to produce bondage;
therefore, from this or that action, there may arise what is unwholesome, wholesome, or both wholesome and unwholesome. (345)
That sovereignty belongs to this Supreme Lord alone;
for this has been determined by me elsewhere at length. (346)
Therefore, enough; let us speak of the subject at hand: this supreme power of action is proclaimed as the "Non-Terrible" (Aghora) aspect of the Lord, for that very reason. (347)
For this very reason, there is courtesy toward these states when they take refuge in Śiva;
for this is the direct path, whereas that which is mere ritual action is not its essence. (348)
"Surely there are no entities here that do not rely on the state of Śiva; they are indeed agents. Being thus instructed, one should comprehend this. (349)
The God of gods is likewise devoid of the path of conceptualization regarding space, time, action, and agent; His power is that which takes on the form of the universe. 350.
That entire universe is also free from the slightest stain of the blemish of time and so forth;
by virtue of His sovereignty, it is autonomous and remains surging within His own self. Since it shines forth from that source, it is also devoid of any exclusion from the immersion into Śiva. (352)
For this very reason, she is the supreme Dakṣiṇā, possessing a non-terrible form, who—as will be stated—bestows the fruit of the abode of Śiva upon the wheel of living beings. (353)
The supreme, non-terrible powers of Śiva are described by the knowers of that [reality] as being elsewhere the power of action (kriyāśakti) residing within bound souls (paśu). 354.
Binding [the breath], established in its own path, and known as the bringer of accomplishment;
that which is proclaimed as the expansion from the letter *a* to the letter *ha*. (355)
That very [Bindu], having resorted to the state of being without vowels (asvara) from its abode in Bindu,
is this entire garland of phonemes, which is the unfolding of the power of action (kriyā-śakti).
By means of this embrace, she who consists of the reflective awareness of "I" remains present; therefore, there is the vibrant manifestation of the full supreme ego-sense (parāhaṃkāra).
He is the devourer of the multitude of bound souls, from Ananta down to Viriñca;
he has drawn into the cavern of his own belly the entire collection of the moving and unmoving worlds.

As long as the mass of individual souls (pudgala) is swallowed within the reflective awareness of one's own consciousness, it remains manifest in the form of the power of action (kriyā-śakti). ||359||

[He is the one] whose state is adorned with a variety of inconceivable and innumerable [manifestations], and whose self consists of the distinctions between peaceful and wrathful forms through the pacification of infinite activities. ||360||
Moreover, due to the propriety of the Bhairava-splendor, which remains well-established as it manifests the greatness of its own devouring, even those of various forms [are absorbed]. ||361||

Possessing the states of being both empty and full—[the reading is *bhavabhavā*]—and variegated by repeated return, they are solely intent upon devouring their own portion, known as the universe, which is the very nature of Śakti. (362)
The powers (śaktis), which have brought about the uprooting of states long established in the world and in time, manifest their respective clusters of rays through their own expansion. (363)
By relying on the reality of the truth of their resolve, they extended [their limbs], which were appropriate for themselves alone and excluded from the worldly conduct of the wicked. (364)
The scriptures indeed coalesce once they have reached their full perfection,
just as it was at the very first arising within the sphere that transcends the world.
In this state where the distinction between the terrified and the liberated has vanished, that very conduct prevails;
here stands the full and great creation of the Supreme Lord.
In her, all those portions of withdrawal and emanation abide in the middle;
it would not be possible to say that she is merely the primordial emanation. (367)
Indeed, how could there be the occurrence of "first" and so forth in that which is without space or time?
This waking state is the primary one, participating in the stage of unfolding. (368)
This Brahmā, whose lotus-seat awakens through a portion of his own power, [emanates] these [energies] starting from the form of Śiva down to that of Brahmā. (369)
Having assumed form, the powers of the Lord of Consciousness manifest;
for although it might be possible to say, "This God is only this much," [or rather, "He is indeed only this much"], (370)
Because the Great Lord, whose nature is consciousness, is immeasurable, it cannot be described;
this has been clearly stated by me in the *Prabodhapañcadaśikā*. (371)
It has been stated that limited luminosity is indeed the defining characteristic of the insentient; for consciousness, being distinct from the insentient, is not so measured. (372)
Nevertheless, such a God himself, though devoid of a human body, by virtue of his own sovereignty, having made himself both moving and unmoving; (373)

For instance, first, by Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, and Sadyojāta, while each was yet desiring to manifest, three divisions were brought forth; and once they had manifested, there are six individual divisions. Furthermore, by these three acting together, one combined division is brought forth: namely, Īśāna and Tatpuruṣa; Īśāna and Sadyojāta; and Sadyojāta and Tatpuruṣa.

Even though they arise together as a dual nature, these three manifest the threefold division. By means of each one of the six—born from Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, and Aghora—and by means of one triad, [the state of] non-Ādhyātma... [is attained]. (Note: The reading is *ekaikaiḥ*.)
[The reading: "By means of three [moments] consisting of two natures. ||374||
The various states of the ten divisions of Śiva (or, according to another reading, the divisions of the Moon) arise;
for this very reason, from the diverse consciousnesses, by virtue of their mutual blending, [these states emerge]. (375)
Even in this [reality] called Śiva, diverse cognitions of duality were produced when there was a conjunction of the left and right among the three faces. (376)
Then, through the future and present manifestations, each will possess its own power;
thus, within the triad of the six, there is a division of Rudras, established in eighteen ways.
Each one has five faces, and from which the face is proclaimed as ten and eighteen; since it is divided into ten and eighteen, its divisions are therefore innumerable. (378)
Since those [beings] are determined according to their various cognitions and actions as previously described, there is no tautology in their case. (379)
For indeed, awakening, conduct, and the sequence of ritual action are each distinct; they are taught in various ways in different contexts, yet all lead to the abode of Śiva. (380)
Just as all droplets of water find rest in the great ocean, so do all acts of knowledge and action find rest in the Great Lord, the ocean of consciousness. 381.
Even the limited water on the earth is indeed drunk up by the rays of the sun, yet it returns again through the medium of rain to the great ocean; likewise,
every knowledge and action in the world clearly proceeds from itself.
And yet, through the tradition of others, it sinks into the ocean of Śiva. ||382||
And that supreme heart-liṅga which is at the end on the right, considered the highest heart,
is also completely filled with all the created states within it. (383)

And because it swallows the portions of light belonging to Māyā—which consists of differentiation and existence—it is black, assuming the form of darkness by virtue of being the destroyer of all things. (384)
For this very reason, it has been stated by the Great Lord in the *Vijñānaśāstra*:
"The entire darkness of the Lord, beginning with [the notion] that space is dissolved in the crown of the head," and so forth. (385)
In this very way, during the long night of the dark fortnight,
one should meditate upon the form of Bhairava, which is difficult for those who practice meditation to comprehend.

And it has been said: "Where there is pleasure, pain, or darkness, or where both are concealed, there is no connection between ignorance and karma, because one perceives dependence and so forth. (387)
Therefore, within this terrifying form that has the appearance of darkness, the four faces shine forth clearly by being completely absorbed within it. (388)

Desiring to emerge, having emerged, desiring to disappear, and having disappeared—in this way, [according to the reading "tataḥ"], this [reality], simultaneously and through its sixteenfold divisions, consists of sixteen aspects. (389)

Entering into Śiva—who is on the right, who is characterized by emission, who is situated in the heart, and who is independent—the scripture known as Bhairava, consisting of eight times eight [chapters], manifests simultaneously. (390)
Thus, the Tantra known as Rudra, Śiva, and Bhairava exists in three ways;
for in reality, this very essence of knowledge unfolds in these three modes. (391)
Through differentiation, through both difference and non-difference, and likewise through the "full" [reading], as well as through the seam of non-difference;
thus, the three primary powers of Śambhu, beginning with Will (icchā), are established. ||392||
In that very context, however, through further elaboration, there is the conjunction with the five powers and so forth;
thus, in the middle, that very triad is distinct, and likewise [the reading is "tathā tatreti"] it is supreme.
This scripture has remained in our teacher’s house through the sequence of oral tradition;
for this very reason, due to its proximity, it possesses the characteristics of both the Left-hand (Vāma) and Right-hand (Dakṣiṇa) scriptures.
The Kaulikī power unfolds at the edge of the limit of the support;
from that [state], she is utterly full, having withdrawn all limiting adjuncts of phenomenal existence.
Bhairava is he whose state is nourished by the surging flow of the ultimate reality (paramārtha)— [the reading "śaktika" is preferred].
In those [directions], namely Īśāna, Vāma, and Dakṣa, there is the triad of powers in due order.
It remains having embraced the triad of powers beginning with Parā;
it manifests the division of duality,
and thus it is called Ananta, the maker of its own manifestation.
They declare that the supreme Lord, whose nature is to swallow all, is in reality indeed Triśiras. ||397||
The Tantras and Kulas of the Upper [tradition], the Left, and those other than these, are for the sake of abandoning the contraction of duality within the two established streams. ||398||

Having as its object the illumination of others, consisting of the threefold meaning, and established in a threefold manner—this very [reality] has been proclaimed by the Supreme Lord under the name Jñānacandra (the Moon of Knowledge). 399.
This entire meaning of the treatise is based on the activity of the supreme word (paravāk), in which distinctions such as the signified and the signifier do not manifest. ||400||

But subsequently, when the Self has manifested through the predominance of the aspect of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), there is the attainment of the sovereignty called *sādākhya*, which consists of the most subtle power of action (*kriyāśakti*). (401)
In the locus of the intermediate [level] of speech (madhyamā), through the yoga of the manifestation of internal discourse, it exists in the form of phonemes, appearing as words and sentences. (402)
In the Svacchanda-śāstra, it is stated by the Lord Sadāśiva himself that he composed the Tantra through sentences consisting of preceding and succeeding words. ||403||
And likewise, it is stated in that very same place regarding the path of the enclosure of Suśiva:
"The enclosure of Suśiva comes first; therein Sadāśiva is to be known. (404)
Endowed with the ten Śivas and accompanied by the eighteen Rudras, his authority resides in the principle of Īśa; however, his desire to grasp that [authority] lies in the principle of Śiva.

In the *varaṇa* [sheath], it is from the point (*bindu*); in the one called *bhoga* [the abode], it is from the manifestation of the All-pervasive Lord; in the *śakti-tattva* of the consciousness known as Bhairava, there is the supreme triad. (406)
Therefore, Sthiti is situated above Īśvara and below the plane of Sadāśiva;
it is described as the enclosure of Suśiva in the venerable Svacchanda-śāsana. (407)

Immediately thereafter, when these divisions of Śiva and Rudra had been fully established upon the path of Māyā, a variety of designations was attained: that which is called "Śiva" by the Śivas, and that which is termed "Rudra" by the Rudras. (The reading *bheda*—meaning "division"—is found in some texts; alternatively, the reading *bhoga*—meaning "enjoyment"—is also encountered.)
Then, through the gradual manifestation of the essence of emerging activity, it becomes clearly manifest. ||409||

The objects of all domains, consisting of phonemes, sentences, and words, are the meanings of the scriptures which rely upon the conventional speech derived from learning that is illusory in nature, and they pertain to the sphere of the world. (410)
They proceed by relying upon those various introductions to the tantras;
therefore, first [one proceeds] as far as the cave of the māyīyā vaikharī. 411.
This meaning of the scripture, composed of illusory syllables, has not arrived;
it is rather the description of the supreme speech, whose sole purpose is the awakening to the internal essence. 412.

In the thirty-seventh [or, according to another reading, the thirty-eighth] chapter, there exists the meaning of the scripture, culminating in the worldly, which is refined by the fundamental impressions (*saṃskāra*) rooted in the unartificial supreme penetration (*parāveśa*) within the all-pervading Lord.
For non-existent entities, there is no reality whatsoever anywhere; how can there be discipline when the sovereign is overcome by lack of discipline? (414)
Therefore, the entire meaning of the scriptures is established as being of the nature of the supreme reality;
consequently, even these [scriptures] such as the Vedas are but rays of the teaching belonging to Māyā.
They manifest solely through the power of Bhairava-Āditya and not from anything else;
for there is never any cause other than the reflective awareness (vimarśa) of consciousness—even if one reads the variant *atyaktāpy evam*. 416.
Consciousness cannot belong to anything other than itself, because it is consciousness alone that exists in such a manner;
thus, the terms "effect" and "cause" are applied to it only as a figurative designation.
For in the transformation of an entity whose nature is to extend gradually [the reading is *dharmiṇaḥ*], it is consciousness alone that appears as the form at both the beginning and the end. (418)
If consciousness were to admit the measurement of time, then clearly we would be eating fragments of the moon from the sky, sliced by a sharp sword. (419)
Therefore, because consciousness does not deviate from its nature as pure awareness and because consciousness is self-luminous, all scriptures are in reality self-luminous. 420.
Nor should it be said that the denotable object exists separately from the denoter, because the denoter itself exists independently as that which will later become the denotable object. (421)
Sometimes the expressive element appears with its own form grasping the expressed object,
while at other times it appears with the manifestation of the universal.
Sometimes, distinguished by proximate and remote qualifiers, it shines forth through the predominance of its clearly manifest essential nature and denotable aspect. ||423||
Therefore, there is sometimes intent upon the meaning, and likewise intent upon the literal form;
in some cases there is the state of desiring to know the meaning, and in others the state consisting of aesthetic flavor (rasa). 424.
The diversity of words is observed because it does not deviate from the nature of consciousness;
what wonder is there that consciousness shines through its manifold expressions? 425.
Thus, sound— which is non-different from the state of reflective awareness whose essence is Śiva— is here the self-luminous manifestation of both itself and others due to its clarity.
That alone is the means of knowledge (*māna*), consisting solely of the reflective awareness that has consciousness as its core.
Furthermore, that [designation] is due to the force of metaphorical usage; for it is thus: ||426||
This ultimate consciousness, which is self-luminous by nature, is declared to be self-awareness (svasaṃvedana), for from it the entire order of the universe is established. ||427||
And this very [consciousness] does not transcend the essential nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
This supreme, full reflective awareness is its enjoyment; it is designated as Paśyantī. (428)

That very goddess is both the supreme (parā) and the non-supreme (aparā); let it be understood that she is "measure" (māna), wherein the object of knowledge (meya), belonging to the aspect of the non-supreme, abides through identity with her. (429)
For the determination of the object of cognition cannot occur through a means of cognition that is distinct from it;
indeed, a crow cannot possess whiteness simply because a swan is white. (430)
And thus the Guru Śaṅkaranandana has said this very thing:
"There is no establishment [of the object] because it is not a means of valid cognition, nor because it is something else, nor because of sublation, nor because of non-existence. (431)

An entity does not attain establishment as an external existence through properties that are inseparable from manifestation and whose nature is restricted to existence; therefore, it is not an [external] entity. (432)
Therefore, the very nature of consciousness itself is grasped as the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge;
its self-luminosity shines forth by its own inherent nature. (433)

And that [cognition], beautiful through the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the word whose essence is the mantra residing within, is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by itself alone, because it lacks dependence on anything else. (434)
The proponents have fashioned various names for that very [reality] through many different modes, all of which arise solely from its grace. (435)
And so, that which is proclaimed as "perception" (pratyakṣa), established by the chisel of the circle of sense-faculties such as the eye, is now being analyzed. (436)
If the existence of the sense organs were established apart from consciousness,
then there would be no unity of the object and its means of cognition, just as in the case of external objects such as jars and the like.

Indeed, the eye and other such organs are the instruments for the self, not jars and the like; therefore, the cognition of entities occurs through those [senses] alone, and not by means of jars and so forth. (438)
Furthermore, since this [mind], which is considered all-pervasive, possesses no distinction in its conjunction [with objects],

and since there is no distinction in its being composed of the elements (bhautikatva), how could there be a fixed fulfillment of the Self's requirement for instruments by means of specific [organs] such as the eye in relation to [specific objects] such as a jar?
A specific kind of conjunction alone is the basis for [something's] being an instrument.
The distinction [between individuals] arises from those various actions proclaimed by the terms "dharma" and "adharma";
this very [distinction] consists of the manifestation of the actual existence of logical reasoning. (441)
Intent on flight, he deceives the simple-minded by saying that [liberation] arises from the power of a self that pervades all conjunctions with the sense organs. (442)
It is called "mind" (manas) because it simultaneously cuts off [the flow of] cognition;
regarding that as well, we say first that the self alone is joined with the mind. (443)
In that case as well, let it be considered: who would bring about the conjunction of the self and the mind?
If it is argued that this [conjunction] occurs because [the self] is all-pervasive, then the mind would reach [all objects] simultaneously with everyone. (444)

If one's own internal mind were the presiding controller that depends upon the eyes and other [senses], then upon the conjunction of even a single sense-organ, everyone would attain omniscience. (445)
Therefore, the basis for objects [is established] through as many portions of the sense-faculties as there are;
it is illuminated by contact with the subtle portions of the faculties that are themselves presided over by the sense-faculties. ||446||
Let an atom of an external object, such as a sacrificial pit or the like, appear;
nevertheless, if it has become the object of the senses through the superintendence of the mind, [it may appear]. (447)
Thus, its very capacity with respect to its own object arises;
for then the rays of the eyes have issued forth through even the most minute apertures. (448)
Why would they not exercise valid cognition regarding the flood of objects existing everywhere?
For the sense organs are indeed fully capable of apprehending objects situated in suitable locations. (449)
Indeed, let the nature of the fitness of a place be investigated:
that place where one who resides there attains realization is said to be fit. (450)
Wherein situated would cognition exist? Or why is this not demonstrated?
Thus, these who consider themselves logicians are devoid of the presentation of valid reasoning. 451.
Why did you not remain silent from the very beginning? What is the use of these boastful claims? This [consequence] follows by force upon one whose own intentions have proven fruitless.
Could the conjunction of the mind and the sense-organ not be improper?
Or rather, does an intention toward that object arise for it? (453)
If [the object] is unknown, what intention could there be? If it is known, what is the use of the contact with the senses?
If it is already perceived, then it must be remembered; and if it is being remembered, it would have been produced by the one who intends. (454)
The effort of one who intends toward one thing arises in relation to another;
[these cognitions] depend upon the sense organs, such as the eye, which are connected to the self and joined with the mind. (455)
How could objects, by the process of transcending the eyes and other senses that have become their immediate conditions, extend the state of being a cognizer within the Self alone? (456)
Surely the status of being a cognizer produced by cognition inheres in the consciousness itself (as the reading *vijñātam* suggests);
therefore, how can there be any suspicion of the status of a cognizer for anything else? (457)
"We say that this alone is knowledge; why indeed would it be otherwise?"—blinded by partiality for his own position, he offered that very same [flawed] answer out of fear. (458)
Just as the mind is said to be the cause when there is contact between the sense faculty and the self, so too let another cause be stated for the contact between the self and the mind. (459)
If that were the case, there would indeed be an infinite regress, which would destroy the very root [of the argument].
Alternatively, the conjunction of the self with its own internal organ must be accepted as being constant. (460)
Those who are always asleep, intoxicated, unconscious, or wretched would be knowers;
yet this kind of knowledge is not desired by you, unlike that of the disciples of the Śākyan.
Therefore, how can that which is called "perceptibility" arise from the range of the sense faculties? Now, this examination of each of these [factors] shall be set forth in detail. (462)
In that regard, [the opponent claims] the mind is atomic, eternal, all-pervading, swift, light, and non-material; yet even this does not attain the status of being established by reason. (463)
If the mind, though subtle and moving swiftly, were to touch its objects repeatedly, then at that very moment the body would become a corpse. (464)

Even while the mind is situated within the body, through the practice of knowledge (jñānayoga), the individual soul (jīva) becomes as small as a single atom; the remainder [of the body] would be like a jar or a wall.

Now, if a connection with one's own internal consciousness has arisen regarding some object within the domain of the self, then that knowledge of the pervasive self is an inherent quality; this constitutes its status as a knower. (466)
If [life] is said to be "born," why is the life-force not established as residing in all bodies?
By this very logic, why would there not be life even in a jar or similar objects? (467)
For knowledge that has arisen regarding an object of discernment exists there only partially;
however, when it concerns the mind within the mere body, its existence would be characterized by parts. ||468||
If the mind were omnipresent, there would be simultaneous cognition of all things; furthermore, if the mind were eternal, cognition would therefore occur at all times. (469)
Even the state of liberation arises only for one who is joined with consciousness;
that there is no union of the self in liberation is truly a great marvel. (470)
For what indeed is excluded from liberation regarding one's own self? [The reading is "is not excluded. And if it is non-material and all-pervading, how could it be the mind? (471)
Since the luminous nature of the eye is indeed accepted solely on account of its skill in manifesting distinguished objects, why is that [mind] not likewise considered material? (472)
If the mind were capable of cognizing all objects, what need would there be for the ostentation of other sense organs?
Surely, its utility regarding external objects occurred previously [when the senses were still required]. (473)
For instance, the subsequent state of the mind occurs when an object has already been perceived by the sense faculty;
regarding this, it is said that [the object] is not grasped by the sense faculty at the very moment prior [to that perception]. (474)
If that [object] is a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), what talk can there be of its being followed later?
Or, if it is merely a universal (*sāmānyamātra*), then that was already grasped previously by the sense faculties. (475)

And at that time, since there is no determination of the individual by means of the mind—[because it is said] "it does not exist"—how could there be a grasping of the universal by means of the mind? (476)
How can there be a perception of a universal without the perception of the individual?
And if there were such a perception of the universal, its capacity to refer to all [individuals] would be obstructed. ||477||
Regarding that entity which has been described as being devoid of the apprehension of specific qualities due to the exclusion of all words, its quality of rapid movement [is established]. //478//
How can the act of going be identical in the case of one's own hand situated in front, a jar located some distance away, and Mount Meru and the like situated at a very great distance? (479)
Because for those things that move swiftly, a distinction is perceived based on their proximity or lack thereof to a previously existing light. (480)
And how could it grasp subtle non-material things such as mountains and the like?
Manifestation is brought about by that which is similar through what is similar. (481)
Granted that there is first the primordial intellect (buddhi), then the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), and then the mind (manas);
even so, the atomicity of the mind is not at all established.
The previously mentioned objections stand fully in force by virtue of their pervasiveness;
thus, the mind [of the opponent] cannot be won over by us through these fragments of reasoning. (483)
Just as it is conceived by those of dualistic vision who are deluded by other philosophical systems,
so too does the light of the conscious self partake in the appearance [or, according to another reading, "the illuminator"] of that very [duality].
Let that power be the mind itself, fashioned by its own autonomy; where there is space, there is the sense of hearing, and therein occurs the perception of all sounds. (485)
Since space is everywhere unobstructed by the eyes and other sense organs,
while merit and demerit constitute the obstruction— [the reading *yuktyupanyāsavaikalī* is corrected to *kevalī*].
And how could deafness and so forth occur, or how could their medical treatment be possible? [The answer is:
through the obstruction of the support of the connection, and likewise through its restoration.
The sense-faculties reside only in their own constituent parts through inherence;
as for space, it is established that it does not reside anywhere at all in a specific manner. (488)
But conjunction (*saṃyogitā*) exists together with being (*bhāva*);
therefore, it too undergoes modification through the benefit or injury [inflicted] upon that [being]. (489)
"That the favor toward that [object] is due to the favor toward its substratum, and thus that [favor] has that [substratum] as its basis"—
this construction of our own words appears to us to be utterly hollow.
For it is clear that the favor toward the sense organs is mediated by their substratum.
When it is asked, "Tell us: what is the substratum for these? [491]

The principle that "that which is the application of favor for this [yoga]—[the reading is 'for this yoga']—is itself its substratum," does not escape the fallacy of circularity (*cakraka*), as it involves mutual dependence. ||492||
That which was described as the tactile sensation whose nature is wind is now analyzed:
the state of wind is established as possessing velocity and remaining unobstructed. (493)
Then, what is the sequence [of reasoning] that there is touch in the region of the body [the reading "in the body" (dehadehe) also exists], but not in a wall?
And the eye is luminous; light has spread forth.
In the external sphere of experience. ||494||
It is now being examined how one knows objects whose primary aspect is form;
for if that light were invisible, how could it be impelled by the mind? (495)
For an instigation that is not cognized can never be logically possible;
nor is a visual light ever known by means of a sense organ. (496)
Furthermore, according to you, the mind is not independent with respect to what is cognized by the sense-faculties;
and if it were unimpelled, it would perceive everything, in every way, and at all times. (497)
There would be an inconsistency regarding either engagement or withdrawal;
moreover, if that light were merely the shape of the eyeball, [it would not illuminate external objects]. (498)
To that extent, there would be apprehension only of what is contained therein, and not of anything else anywhere;
likewise, this is the opposite when the eyeball itself is closed.
Or else, when [the eyes] are opened, there would be apprehension of every object;
for when the eye is opened and the circle of rays has spread forth.
For him, there is no concealment as there is for one looking at a cloth when his eyes are closed;
therefore, why would the perception of an object not occur for one whose eyes are closed? (501)
In the midst of thick darkness, for one whose eyes are closed, there is the appearance of variegated light; and likewise for one whose pair of eyes is afflicted by that [light]. (502)
How could that [perception] occur for yogins when there is darkness before their eyes?
Even if their eyes were opened, there would be no apprehension of objects anywhere. (503)
Through the application of mental superintendence, there is an expansion exceeding [the size of] atoms;
and as for its dependence upon a lamp, why is that not also contradicted? (504)
The light of a lamp is beneficial for the internal self, the eyes, and objects;
it does not, however, serve as a refinement for each individual mental modification. If that were the case, [it would follow that]... 505.
When a lamp is being prepared at night, there would be the apprehension of its form;
for if it were the refinement of the self, that [apprehension] would occur because of the self's omnipresence. (506)
Since conjunction and refinement would result in the cognition of form at all times, what other kind of refinement can be said to exist for that which is formless and eternal? (507)
If it is argued that there is assistance to the eye, then, since the light-ray resides in the region of the eye,
a form situated in the midst of that light would never be perceived.
But surely, that multitude of ocular rays does not reach the location of the object;
alas, why then should consciousness not arise right there at its own location? (509)

Since the self exists in that very body by virtue of its omnipresence, and the instruments [of action] exist in that very place, it is therefore a vain assertion to say that "the body is the locus of experience" or "it is the living being. (510)
When the movement of the rays of the eyes has been established, it is clear that [the path] begins from one's own hand along the unobstructed forest track. (511)
How indeed could the perception of the sun, the moon, and so forth arise, since even though they move swiftly, the aforementioned distinction between being distant and not distant [remains]? (512)

When that [object] is covered by the two—namely, the lamp and the eye—how could there be a cognition of the object as being purely pure, given that it is possessed of a state of being obscured by those two? (513)
Blindness and its treatment are not [possible] if there is a corruption of the locus;
and if the tongue were of the nature of water, then that water would flow out from it. (514)
Then how can there be stability for it, and what is the manifestation of its various flavors?
For while it is joined with the state of a single flavor, that [manifestation] does not abide in a state of multiple flavors. (515)
There would be no cognition of a single taste, just as when there is an excess of bile, the functioning of the sense of taste is not capable of perceiving sweetness. (516)
Objection: Is it not the case that pungency resides in bile, whereas it does not reside thus in the tongue?
If so, then bile and molasses would be identical [the reading is *tulyam*] in their reaching the path of the tongue. (517)
Thus, there would be a simultaneous cognition of both bitterness and sweetness;
for if the tongue were devoid of taste, how could it manifest flavors? (518)
If it is argued that this [smell] exists by its own nature, then what is the reason for this insistence on its being watery?
Furthermore, the nose is composed of earth; why is its solidity not perceived? (519)
Now, one might object: "Does that fragrance, which is characterized by an abundance of the quality of smell, not manifest?
It does not, because there is no such valid cognition [of it] as possessing a fragrance made manifest by a sense faculty. (520)
The mind, which is not of the nature of earth and is devoid of smell, is indeed capable of apprehending odor;
therefore, for you, an inference of such a [mind] is not possible. (521)

Therefore, it is not tenable that the aggregate of the sense-faculties is composed of the primary elements (bhautika). However, if they are derived from the ego-principle (āhaṅkārika), then their pervasiveness and indivisibility [are established]. (522)
Furthermore, there is a contradiction regarding its dependence on the body, and it does not exist as an instrument;
let that pentad of organs of action, beginning with speech, be analyzed. (523)
That particular essence of speech, which arises from the impact of the vital breath extending from the navel to the crown of the head, is described here as being of such a nature.
Sound would be its effect; let it be considered who here is the agent.
The self certainly lacks agency, even if that were so, because of its omnipresence. (525)
When the sound is uttered by me, why are you not born as the speaker?
Even in the case of primordial matter (prakṛti), this same defect applies: it would be devoid of agency while being the agent.
There is no stability in the instrument [of speech], even when the vocal organ is equal;
how then does the state of being indistinct or very clear arise in sounds? (527)
And how could there be a distinction residing in the sound during whispered conversation, recollection, and so forth?
If it is due to effort, then since even effort arises [from something else], how could that [distinction] come from it? (528)
For indeed, a different [result] arises, not one produced from the qualities of another;
by means of which [result], the [defect] is counteracted through the intensity or mildness of the effort. (529)
If the hand-faculty does not take [an object], how can there be grasping by means of the mouth and so forth?
And what could be called "grasping," if it is intended as "appropriation"? (530)
The making of one's own is called "appropriation" (svīkāra).
If the word "own" (sva) denotes the self (ātman), then the self would be the primordial nature (prakṛti). (531)
Since there is nothing at all that is non-material (aprākṛta), how indeed can there be a lack of self-nature?
Furthermore, if the ego (ahaṅkāra) were the self, then the ego would not possess the activity found in a jar.
This [object] belongs to the self, and it is corrupted by this very same defect;
for indeed, everything that is related to the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) is its own. (533)
For the all-pervading self, there exists neither anything that belongs to it nor anything that does not belong to it;
such is the same logical progression for the sense of touch as well. (534)

Furthermore, that which is called "going" by virtue of reaching another place from one place is established as being of the nature of abandonment, precisely through the absence of appropriation. //535//
This act of acceptance is also refuted; even that aspect of acceptance which exists in the act of going, its appropriate instrument is the sense organ of the hand, not that called the foot. (536)
For in this way, a confusion of the functions of the sense-faculties arises;
therefore, by those who know the great logic, in the final system, [it is so stated]. (537)
A great deal of fine-sounding rhetoric has been uttered to prohibit motion:
"That which has already gone is not being gone over; that which has not yet gone is likewise not being gone over. (538)
In one's own system, it is stated that there is nothing such as "departing" or "arriving," and so forth;
furthermore, the anal faculty is not merely a cavity, due to the movement of the internal wind. (539)
Indeed, emission (utsarga) is said to be their common function; by that, such is the established state.
And whatever the organ of generation (upastha) may be, its function is now described. (540)
In that case, pleasure itself would be called "pleasure" even when it is pain;
likewise, let it be explained that even in delusion, it is merely another sense-faculty. (541)
Whether seen, touched, smelled, or even heard, bliss is experienced therein; therefore, another sense organ must indeed be named [to account for it]. (542)

Furthermore, that faculty which is designated as "pleasure" functions there [in the state of cessation] like the anus; it is not logical for it to be included among the five faculties of action. (543)

If the arising of cognition occurs simultaneously for the entire web of sense organs and mental faculties, then why is there not simultaneous awareness even when [only] the mental faculty is active? (544)
And if there is no simultaneity when seeing reality with the eye, why is it not possible for [the eye] to be obstructed by subtle pearls and the like? (545)
If the tactile faculty were not present when the visual faculty is directed toward objects, how could there be no grasping, moving, and so forth for one whose eyes are closed? (546)
One should determine that one's own body is like a wall;
moreover, apart from the sense organs, nothing called "body" is found.
The sense organs would have to be of the nature of touch; why indeed would they not be so?
If the body were the regulator, it could not exist anywhere except where the sense organs are present. (548)
And how could there be perception by the sense-faculties even of non-material entities?
Or why would there not be perception of pleasure and so forth in exactly the same way? (549)
Furthermore, color-form is not [the object] because it is perceived even by touch;
nor is touch [the object] because it is accessible to the eye. How, then, could there be a perception of these two? (550)
Whether by means of touch or by sight, let action also be considered in this way;
for in that manner, there is the manifestation of universals, inherence, and so forth, as well as of the whole.

How could formless things and the like be perceived by the collection of sense faculties? For such [perception] arises from contact born of either conjunction or inherence, as was the case initially. (552)

Those who assert that inherence (*samavāya*) is a real entity (*bhāva*) perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) fall, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), into both the error of non-implication and the error of over-extension.
For what kind of proximity could there be for these [tastes] with this [visual] sense-organ?
[There is none], because the two parts—the juice and the form of the wood-apple—are related through inherence in a common substrate (saṃyuktasamavāya). ||554||
If they are indeed equal, why is taste not perceived by the eye?
Or how, according to you, can non-existence be grasped by the eye? (555)
The claim that "it exists" because it is necessarily an entity is also refuted;
for even inherence (*samavāya*) is indeed an entity, yet proximity does not exist in it.
And yet there is perceptibility; therefore, all that is inconsistent.
Is it not the case, however, that "existence" (bhāvatva) is conceived through connection with a universal? (557)
And since it would also reside in inherence—as the reading is "it resides in the three categories and in inherence"—how could that be?
Alas! Therefore, it is not logical for existence (bhāvatva) to reside in a universal.
In that case as well, what is the use of the obsession with proclaiming proximity?
For [universals] such as generality and inherence would be perceived even without sensory contact. (559)
Among all things that exist in the world, why indeed should there not be such a perception?
Is this not simply the inherent nature of things, and does it not deserve no further questioning? (560)
Surely the discourse on logic is exhausted; therefore, enough with these dogmatic certainties!
Thus, there is no grasping of the rule of connection for inference.

And how could there be positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) without the apprehension of that [universal]? How [could one grasp] all the individual instances of smoke and non-smoke, or fire and non-fire? (562)
Furthermore, how could they be grasped by birth alone, or through their lineage and so forth? [The reading is "grahyantāsatvayādyatayeti.
Surely, the apprehension of the relationship must occur through the connection with a universal (sāmānya). ||563||
We do not know this; you ought to make it known:
where there is the generality of smoke, is there also the generality of fire? (564)
In this case, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) if it were merely a matter of extension [of properties], because of its omnipresence (vibhutva);
however, it is not logical [to apply it] to an individual or a location, as in the case of fire residing in a particular instance of smoke.

The nature of a specific instance of smoke is fire, and the nature of fire is its inseparability from a specific instance [of smoke]. From what means of valid cognition is this known? If it is from perception, then how is that so? (566)

From what source is there the comprehension of the rule that other individual instances likewise possess that nature? And as for that universal "smokeness" which is desired here as the restrictive factor; [it is untenable]. (567)
In that case, the universal "fire-ness" exists as an inseparable concomitant;
for it is not logical to claim that a universal does not exist without another universal. (568)
If it is understood by that [means], then this is characterized by inseparable connection (avinābhāva);
however, in the understanding of inseparable connection, one falls into the fallacy of mutual dependence (anyonyāśrayatā). //569//
If the cognition of the universal "fire-ness" were to arise from smoke,
then there would be no dependence upon the individual instance when grasping that universal.
And once a universal has been determined to be distinct from individuals, the claim that it inheres in them is merely the manifestation of the faith of the deluded. (571)

And if the universal were a separate entity and performed causal efficiency by means of that [particular], there would be no activity on the part of the world, for the world is intent upon attaining that [utility]. (572)
Now, if it is argued that the universal is perceived as implying the individual, then since the universal is already known, why would it be so preoccupied as to imply the individual? (573)
And who indeed would believe that its occurrence took place in that [past] time?
For there is a difference between the two types of universals (jāti) established by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). ||574||
Since there is no apprehension [of the object] through differentiation, the functioning [of the senses] is therefore postulated;
thus, this shameless person deceives children of dull intellect. (575)
"One deluded by the conceit of being clever even deceives us;
thus it was truly said by someone who perceives the ways of the world. (576)
That by which the virtuous person feels shame, by that the non-virtuous person is pleased.
There is no apprehension through differentiation; in this regard, whatever is apprehended is considered to be "if there is apprehension" (the reading being *ced-grahaṇam*). //577//

And that which is considered here in the phrase "the establishment of the means of valid cognition through differentiation"—by the mutual contradiction between those two, the very thesis is subverted. (578)
If those two were distinct from the means of cognition, why would there not be a perception of that distinction?
For whatever means of cognition perceives difference is itself the apprehension of difference. (579)

When it is said that there is no apprehension by way of difference, it would also follow that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing difference; therefore, the cognition of reality is not of this nature.

And since cognition exists through the individual instance and so forth in the case of verbal testimony and inference, why should that [cognition], which has a universal as its object, not be a grasper of difference? (581)
Now, is it not the case that the nature of a universal (jāti) as it appears in perception does not appear in the same way when a cognition is produced by means of words or logical marks? (582)
If there is indeed the occurrence of properties such as being manifest or unmanifest within the universal (jāti), then those qualities must likewise reside in the generalities (sāmānyas). ||583||
But surely, such a cognition appearing as something distinct and vivid would be unreal;
for cognition is established solely through the manifestation of the form of its object. (584)
Indeed, its clarity and other qualities are metaphorically attributed [to it] through the clarity and so forth produced by the coloring of the object;
however, its own intrinsic clarity and such are like those of the rays of the sun.

Let it not be so; for by those various non-luminous atoms of fire that are distinct from it, the [luminous atom] becomes interspersed and internalized, resulting in a state of flickering and dimness. (586)
Existence and non-existence manifest as being merely constructed through origination;
such a similarity is not well-founded in partless consciousness which is devoid of qualities. (587)
For an object appears only through the arising of cognition;
it does not appear when [cognition] does not arise, nor does it appear clearly in any other way. (588)

Now, whether in the case of verbal cognition or inference, does the universal not appear by its own nature? Since it thus implies the individual, how can there be a perception of it as distinct [from the individual]? (589)

It is said that the universal, by means of its luminous form, implies the individual; that cognition of it which occurs while residing in the individual is itself called "implication" (ākṣepa). //590//
In that case, would there not be an identity between all cognitions by means of the perceiver?
Surely that manifestation is indistinct; let this very point be analyzed. (591)
If there were two properties, namely clarity and lack of clarity, then that universal would be established as residing in the manifestation of what is not clear. (592)
Nevertheless, the apprehension of such a thing remains clearly evident;
moreover, a universal cannot possibly be inherent in things that possess manifest individuality. (593)
"Is it not the case that what is called a 'universal' is said to reside in mere individuality?
Even with our minds well-composed, we do not understand the meaning of the word 'mere' (mātra) here. (597)
For that [object] must be either an individual, or a universal, or neither of the two.
But surely, if it is an individual, what would be the purpose of an implication here? (598)

Could it be that there are no real entities at all that conform to your assertions? Furthermore, as for the refutation based on [differences in] state, place, time, and so forth that has been discussed—[is that also not applicable]? (599)
In this inference, the wise person should also follow that which was stated by Hari;
moreover, it is possible to render every reason (hetu) inconclusive.
Just as in the case of a corporeal object, it is certain that "smoke may exist even without fire"—
what proof is there for the claim that "all smoke is necessarily connected with fire"? (601)
Nor is the presence of another means implied by the fact that [the reason] functions through a commonality;
for why would smoke not be a prover of fire even in the case of corporeality? (Or, according to the reading *mūrtatāpi*: "even in the case of being corporeal") [602].
In the production of the cognition that establishes the necessity of impermanence, there is neither mutual dependence nor infinite regress; for indeed, it is not so. (603)
It is not tenable to say that [the object] "subsides" in this way through the means of cognition that is inference;
for those who maintain the distinction between the two [means of cognition], these two [inference and verbal testimony] are simply not applicable as valid cognitions.
But sound and the like have been definitively ascertained by the wise through inference;
therefore, this [consciousness] exists solely as self-awareness by virtue of its self-luminosity. //605//
This manifestation shines forth through the manifold elaborations of the knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and so on;
it is a radiance like the shimmering of thick waves upon the ocean, a moonlight that acts as a companion in the blooming of the night-lotus petals. [Nirveda...]
[The reading:
That expansion which occurs in supreme consciousness through the intermingling of the means of knowledge, the object, and the knower—this is the manifold art of conceptualization in the world. (606)
Therefore, this very Light, thoroughly replete with manifold powers, shines by itself in diverse forms everywhere and in every way. (607)

Thus, this [consciousness], appearing clearly through the path of worldly forms and so forth, receives the designation "perception" (pratyakṣa) due to its own power, arising from what is called conceptualization (vikalpa). //608//
For instance: the partiality of the God of gods is the opening of that vision (or, according to another reading, the partiality of the body);
the vibration of the vital breath is its one-pointedness; and mental state is the accumulation of its qualities. ||609||
Thus, it is clear that everything which appears is perception;
however, in this case, there is no application of categories such as agent, object, instrument, or cause.
But surely this [consciousness] exists on the subsequent path of conceptualization;
for while the appearance of the body and the jar is clear at first, it becomes unclear later. (611)
That very [consciousness], however, when its form is concealed, is the self-awareness of the pure aspects;
from that arises the manifestation of the body and the jar, and even there, this same process prevails.
Even in that case, where there is the manifestation of millions of billions of bodily forms,
if there is no such expansion [of consciousness] either before or after, [then it is not true manifestation].
It reaches the stage of reflective awareness, variegated by being both manifest and unmanifest;
yet that very [reality] is one alone, whose nature is the full manifestation of its own essence.
This manifold manifestation of Śiva’s light does not exist in reality;
rather, its diversity is perceived there through the immersion into forms that are not its true nature.
Furthermore, entry into that which is not of the nature of Śiva’s light is not logical; or else, by the force of the reasoning already stated, there is no diversity anywhere. (616)
However, appearing as something variegated, it produces a variegated state; thus, this Caitra appears to us in such a way, like a painting [the reading "cittavadbhāvam īdṛśam" is also found]. (617)
Enough with that view of Maitreya; he who sees me as one who perceives reality, seeing thus, is one perfected in meditative concentration.
Indeed, in previous tens of millions of births, he experienced various forms of suffering and the like;
yet even he who has come by this path shall be liberated through meditation, spiritual conduct, and other means.
Even that other [subject] who possesses liberation arises in this way without end;
yet this light is one alone, which for a long time has not been divided.
For this very reason, there exists no distinction whatsoever that could divide Maheśvara, who is non-dual, beautiful with light and bliss; [the reading "saṃprabhedet" is also found]. (621)
If place, time, form, cognition, properties, limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and so forth, which are accepted as differentiators, appear [as such], then that appearance is "distinction" (*vibhā*). 622.
If that [reality] is indeed such a non-difference, then this non-duality (advaita) is manifest;
the word "difference," however, is merely devoid of any objective counterpart.
Or let there be a conceptualization of difference that arises within the manifestation;
nevertheless, by the logic already stated, it will find its foundation in that very [manifestation] itself.
This jar and this cloth are distinct from one another;
they are distinct from other cognizers, and they are also distinct from me. (625)
Thus, this one Light is likewise of the nature of reflective awareness (amarśa).
[Objection: But if this is so, is this not partiality? How can there be non-duality for you? (626)
Let there even be difference; what indeed cannot be endured directly?
This is merely an attempt to promote song and instrumental music among a gathering of deaf people.
For we do not assert that non-duality is established by the sublation of the appearance of duality;
for if that were so, it would indeed be an acceptance of your own position, since duality is very clearly evident. (628)
"This is duality, this is not"—wherein both this and that, as well as duality and non-duality, shine forth equally, that is declared to be non-duality (advaya). ||629||
"Let it be so; let there even be difference. We are not seekers of words.
Let this [difference] exist, for it is neither to be rejected nor accepted by us, just as it is for you in this matter. (630)
If you wish to embrace the side that benefits all beings,
then you should take refuge in the great shelter of the supreme non-dual vision.
This will be the eighteenth principle in the section on authority;
may that which is to be attained at the end be the ultimate reality.
In this regard, those who have not found rest rely upon limited consciousness;
they are utterly afflicted by the delusions arising from birth and death. (633)
Therefore, that very light is the one Supreme Lord;
it is by that very light itself that [the world] shines as "perception. (634)
There, all those views necessarily enter [the ocean] like great rivers into the sea; once they have entered, they attain the state of having accomplished their purpose.

For instance, the causal complex of mental cognition arises from form, light, and the mental organ, together with the cognizer and the object of cognition, or excluding one of them, in various ways. (636)
