"The authority [of the scriptures] belongs to those who dwell within the limits of the earth, as determined by destiny;
others, however, say that this distinction is due to the fact that time itself revolves. (807)

This present [moment], whose nature is manifest, proceeds [or, according to another reading, "ceases"]; however, at that time, the portion of its nature that has already passed away consists of non-manifestation. (808)
An entity that is already existent is conceived as something yet to be produced through the postulation of causes;
yet this [entity] is not independent, because they are mutually dependent. (809)

Because it does not remain fixed, because it is observed as a transformation of form, because there is no attainment of a finite limit, and because it depends on both the subject and the object; ||810||

Because it is devoid of the manifestation of that nature free from limiting conditions (upādhi), and because a nature that is either unitary or manifold, or eternal or non-eternal, is logically untenable. ||811||
Because a single substratum is one, even when its substrate is concealed;
and because time is of no use when there is a distinction within the action itself. ||812||

Because there would be an infinite regress whether [the distinction] is produced by that [upādhi] or by another through mutual dependence, and because the appearance of difference based on limiting adjuncts (aupādhika-bheda) is unreal and non-ultimate; ||813||
Because an effect would be impossible [otherwise], because a single [moment] is of no use, and because consciousness possesses a vividness that confers the status of "present" upon it. (814)
Therefore, because of the dissolution of the past and the future, as well as the dissolution of the present,
this Lord, who is Consciousness alone, fully manifests time.
Thus, for this consciousness whose nature is self-luminous, there is the cycle of transmigration known as the appearance of time;
it contains its own manifestation within itself, consisting of both existence and non-existence among all entities. (816)
Abiding in form is said to be the manifestation of subjectivity; this is not "I," nor is "I" this; and this is not that, nor is that this. ||817||
"This is that" is a wonder: the status of being a means of knowledge belongs only to the manifestation of non-existence.
That supreme subjectivity which is pure—within it, there is a separate state. (818)
What is the use of that [consciousness] being isolated in this respect—that there is no pride?
For all this worldly state of being a subject (*mātṛbhāva*) is of such a nature. (819)
In that regard, non-existence (abhāva) possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and that [status] arises through the grace of time;
for thus is he complete, assuming the form of the essence of all things.
Where is the measure, where is the object of measurement, and where could the measurer abide?
For if the measure and the other factors were real, their existence could not be relative.

Furthermore, the existence of fatness and so forth, or of a mother and so forth, can never be established, because that [existence] is impossible whether one obtains or does not obtain the nature of the other. ||822||

Furthermore, because it would lead to the over-extension [of the definition] everywhere due to the possession of omniscience and so forth, and because reality does not arise simultaneously for those who do not benefit [from it], [it cannot be established]. (823)

In the case of motherhood and so forth produced by another object of cognition and so on, that state [of motherhood] also remains established as being equal to the unarisen, precisely because it arises from something other than that. ||824||
Therefore, that Śiva, who is the perfect conscious self, while fragmenting his own part, may also conceive this portion of duality such as "I am not" and so forth. (825)
Therefore, within that extent of myself, I am the totality of everything other than that;
consequently, even the notion "I am not" arises from something else as a means of withdrawal.
Both of these "this-constituents" (idamaṃśau) mutually exclude one another;
the "this-constituent" residing in the intellect conceals its own "I-constituent" (ahamaṃśa).
It remains [inactive] and does not cause this [object] to move, like a pot covered by a cloth; for it is thus dependent upon the intellect, being bound by convention. (828)

This [notion of "I"] arises from the internal synthesis [of the aggregates], by excluding the portion that is not "I," and from the exclusion of the collection of teeth and other parts that are not the portion of "I," it is the "I" within.
Through the exclusion of "I am this," there is the manifestation of the mutual exclusion of "I am that";
it is by depending upon these six deities, whose nature is emptiness, that [consciousness] proceeds. (830)

The cognition that "this is that very same thing" is called a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); it is by means of this that time is calculated, through the arising of its own creative power (*kalā*) over the universe. (831)
In this regard, that which exists here as a portion of light, self-luminous, is, by its nature as a positive entity, the very soul that vitalizes all things. (832)
He is not designated as the mother, nor as the means of knowledge, nor as the object of knowledge;
rather, through his union with emptiness, he is the non-existence whose presiding deity is Rudra. (833)
That very [consciousness] attains the status of a means of knowledge (māna) through its association with that which is to become the knower;
and it has been thus established that the object of knowledge (meyam) is not distinct from the means of knowledge. ||834||
In this manner, some who were disciples of the venerable teacher known as Bhavatrāta have established the nature of time here. (835)

Thus, in the Person (puruṣa), who is radiant with the joy of the manifestation of the attribute of consciousness, there exists that which is called the "sixfold sheath" (kañcuka-ṣaṭka), said to bestow the state of being a subject (mātṛtva). 836.
Some maintain that each one [of the means of knowledge] possesses validity; others, however, consider that only one [of them], when accompanied by all the others, does so. (837)
Some [apply] at some time, for someone, somehow, or somewhere;
others apply to two by twos, and others through the application of groups of three. (383)
Some [attain it] through mutual assistance, others through awakening by one another,
while yet others [attain it] through the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇasāmya), [perceiving] primordial nature (prakṛti) itself as the means of knowledge.
They know [the subject] to be primary because of the observation of states such as sleep, intoxication, and fainting;
for wherever this cognizer exists, he remains as if asleep. (840)

This very state constitutes its "motherhood," because the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge are not perceived [as distinct], and because they are mutually unmodifiable even when such a state is in a state of deep sleep. (841)
This very nature (prakṛti) alone conceives the notion "I know";
however, the primary authority regarding that [knowledge] is the perception by the Puruṣa alone. (842)
And some, relying on the cloak of Sāṃkhya, maintain that this [Self] is pure, changeless, and devoid of the nature of both existence and non-existence. (843)
Others say that in the house of the teacher named Vayya, who lived by means of knowledge, there exists only the ground of the intellect, colored by the seer and the seen. (844)

Some authorities of the supreme sages consider the means of valid cognition to be the collection of their functions; others know the entire range of phenomena to be numbered as eightfold, beginning with dharma.
Some say it is indeed the ego (ahaṃkāra), some the intellect (dhī), and others the mind (manas);
some consider all three of these to be identical everywhere. (846)
Others have assigned each of these to one of the ten sense organs;
some, however, assign them all, because they function everywhere with an unmanifested state of intent.

For even in one who is blind, there exists a certain portion of the sense-base of form which, upon contact with one ear, undergoes a transformation while remaining situated within the other eye. (848)
"Daybreak has arrived, adorning the circle of the sky with clouds dissolved away"—hearing this, the blind man attains supreme joy on a winter day. (849)
Even though he infers the pleasure produced by the warding off of cold,
nevertheless his own self-awareness does not manifest that [pleasure] as its form.
Others have maintained that the sense-faculties consist of mere subtle elements (tanmātra), based on such scriptural injunctions as "the visual ray does not touch [its object]. (851)
For this very reason, the invisibility of the eyes and other sense organs is logically consistent;
however, their invisibility with respect to a yogin can never be logically established.
Others, however, have declared that gross elements and luminous bodies possess the nature of means of knowledge;
while still others have maintained that even the object of cognition possesses the status of a means of knowledge. (853)
The established rule is that whatever constitutes motherhood is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Therefore, since jars and other such things possess that [nature], they too are traditionally known as means of valid cognition.
And worldly designation does not follow from the nature of reality;
for, being constructed by mere whim, it is for the most part merely figurative. (855)
When questioned, "How do you know, sir? and "I know that," he replies, "I know by means of this perceived jar. (856)
Therefore, even regarding the object of cognition, it is certainly not the case that being a means of knowledge is not worldly;
furthermore, when the doctrine of non-difference is firmly established as the root principle, contradiction is no longer a defect.

But those who say that the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is its causal complex (sāmagrī), by them too it is clearly intended that the status of being a means of valid cognition belongs to the object and so forth; otherwise, how could it exist even in a collection? (858)
Others, however, maintain that for every such distinction of number and magnitude,
there is a means of knowledge arising either sequentially in all cases or sometimes non-sequentially.
In some places, it is beautiful due to its fullness in swallowing both the sequential and the non-sequential;
that doctrine is now briefly presented for consideration. (860)
First, by means of the connection with the object of cognition, which appears instantaneously and is entirely concealed by the intention of perceiving other objects; (861)
In that state, the final manifestation is the motherhood of the eye;
thereafter follows the intensely radiant expansion of the group consisting of the mind, ego, and intellect.
From that arises the state of shining with consciousness purified by the masculine [principle];
from that, one gradually causes the nights of ignorance—consisting of time, its divisions, and passion—to fade away.
Otherwise, or equally, or by means of pairs, or in groups of three, or entirely,
or even through the combination of four or five [factors], [this occurs] in the state of Āṇava.
Furthermore, doubts known as "non-existence," "agency," "attachment," "proof," and "reasoning" indeed arise therein, variegated by their respective sequences. (865)
Following that, this non-conceptual [awareness], which manifests pure sovereignty,
attains the status of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) when it abides in the final state of valid knowledge.
Then, resting in the support of the vast powers of knowledge and will belonging to Sadāśiva,
he becomes the Mother (Mātā) and attains fullness, perfectly at peace within the path that culminates in Śakti.

Since full subjectivity manifests in this way, [the various states of consciousness] arise from the separation caused by the concealment of one or another of its constituent parts. (Note: The reading *tadanyamatā* is also found.)
Due to the distinctions of clarity, otherness, and difference, cognitions have reached a state beyond numbering.
For this very reason, those who do not understand the condition proclaimed in the Śiva-scriptures [err]. (869)

In cognitions that are clear or unclear, in the domain of memory and non-memory, and in states such as deep sleep, rapidity occurs because of the impossibility of reflective awareness (*amarśa*) and the like through logical reasoning. (870)

"Attention of the mind," "volitional formation," and "the conceptualization of the unseen [karmic] factors such as dharma"—these words are indeed clear; what meaning does the word *tatra* have here? (871) Furthermore, since the validity of the entire series of higher and higher principles has been established, [what is the point of further inquiry?]
A portion of each successive lower level of reality assumes the status of an object of cognition. ||872||
And there is no sequence here, because it is possible for there to be an interval;
for knowledge does not fail to examine the cognition that is produced by the intellect. (873)
Knowledge is said to be the discerning faculty, for it rests upon the back of the intellect;
its nature is luminous, while the external [sense] consists of the perception by the sense organs. (874)

They say that the mind (manas) exists for the purpose of volition, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) for the purpose of self-assertion, the intellect (dhī) for the purpose of determination, and knowledge (vidyā) for the purpose of discernment. (875)

In that very [consciousness], he perceives passion as the coloring agent, limited power (kalā) as the indicator of capacity, time (kāla) as the divider, and necessity (niyati) as the regulator. ||876||
[The cognition] touches upon that which appears as common to other mothers, while discerning the various forms of both the object-mandala and its perceiver. (877)
Māyā causes the agitation of falling away from the enjoyment of fullness;
Sadvidyā bestows repose in fullness and consists of the nature of the auspicious Śiva. ||878||

[He worships] the power of will (icchā-śakti), which discerns the essential nature of the aspect of existence filled with knowledge, and which manifests the state of fullness belonging to the aspect of the subject. ||879||
Depending upon this, the full nature of the Mother unfolds:
first as luminous perception, and thereafter as the intended conceptualization.
Subsequently, there is the observation of certainty, discernment, non-attachment, non-duality, the cessation of the locus of agency, and the manifestation of commonality. ||881||

The full perception of the object of knowledge, which is filled with the non-disturbance of various reflections, as well as the consciousness of being a perfect subject, is indeed the state of Bhairava. (882)
In this way, as long as he manifests that which consists of the sixteen objects of knowledge, so long is this moon of consciousness said to abide in the state of the eighteen digits (kalās). ||883||
The supreme state is first bliss, then desire, and then mastery; emergence and the onset of diminution—thus the group of six is established. (884)

Beginning from the unsurpassed [state] and ending with the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), such as this is the very will (*icchā*) that, through the power of lordship (*īśana*), abides as the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).
Apprehending even a slight fragment of the state of manifestation, it becomes neuter;
and as for [the powers] beginning with Will, they arise from the union with the preceding and the unsurpassed Bliss.
Then, through the conjunction of initial and final sounds, the four diphthongs arise;
thereafter, from the attainment of the awareness of one's own essential nature, there occurs the state of the bindu and the rest.
Then, within that which possesses a form filled with the entire composition, there is indeed the emission belonging to Śakti, which is known as "projection" (vikṣepa). ||888||
The seventeenth digit is the separation of emission itself;
in some cases, that same [digit] becomes the eighteenth through the application of further agitation. (889)
This supreme Kaulikī Śakti, who belongs to the Akula, is the transcendent (parā) power of the unsurpassed form that has the nature of Parabhairava. 890.
This very emission is that [Supreme Lord]; from it this world is born.
Its fitness for agitation is the arising of the creative process of agitation. (891)
Because it is devoid of the state of agitation and fullness, it does not descend into the sequence of Akula;
thus, it arises from the oscillation of self-reflection whose nature consists of the sixfold group. 892.
Because its nature is non-transgression, it is the unfolding of the very first [state];
that alone is the Blessed One, whose essence eternally flashes forth within. (893)
He whose central power is filled with the flood of all internal states, who is beautiful with the bliss of the world arising from the nature of the agitation of his own will; ||894||
That union of Śiva and Śakti, eternally throbbing and beautiful with the essence of the full visarga, is designated as "affection" (sneha). ||895||
In this very state of the full emission (pūrṇavaisarga), in order to attain entry, they practice the oral tradition beginning with licking, churning, and so forth. 896.
For thus, presiding over the central channel (madhyamā-nāḍī), the supreme radiance, having become intensely agitated by the flow of the seasonal fluids (ṛtu-madya), vitalizes the entire body. (897)
That which attains the state of emission reaches the wonder of bliss;
however, that [emission] alone is incomplete, whereas that which consists of the Lord is complete.
Therefore, this single power of emission unfolds;
indeed, emission itself becomes agitated due to the doubling of effort. (899)
The letter *ha* is the progenitor of all consonants;
and it, moreover, through union with the *bindu*, returns to its own very ground. (900)
That ego-sense (ahaṃbhāva) which relies upon the supreme is intended here [as the letter *a*];
right here, that which is born from the vowel *a* is called *kākhya*, while the other is born from the vowel *i*. (901)
For from that very [source], the dental class (*ṭavarga*) arises from the letter *ṛ* through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the shadow of the phoneme *r*;
and thereafter, it proceeds from the earth (*dharā*) through the sequence of its shadow-limiting adjuncts.
The *tavarga* follows that [the *tavarga*], and after it come the *u*-vowels, *ra*, *la*, and *va*;
likewise, from the *i*-vowel group and the *u*-vowel group, they follow in sequence—precisely for this reason. (903)
The semi-vowels (*antaḥsthā*) are eight, and from the *i*-vowels there are two divisions;
the emergence of *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s* occurs through their conjunction with the pure limiting adjuncts (*upādhikalā*). (904)
For the entire manifold creation exists as an emanation of desire alone; therefore, it is only logical that it possesses the nature of being established in various forms. (905)

Since this state of being solidified, which consists of the womb, belongs to the individual soul (jīva) alone, it is that very thing which is here defined as the power (śakti) of the Supreme Lord. 906.
Right there, the internal principles [are established] according to the sequence of the stages of Parāvāc:
the principle of Śiva is in the *a*-group, while from *ka* up to *ha*, it extends to the end of Śiva.
Thus, this "sandwiched" (saṃpuṭa) yoga, consisting of thirty topics, has been described.
In this way, the Goddess of Consciousness would clearly become full and undivided. (908)
Everything would exist within her, and she would likewise exist everywhere;
for he who sees me everywhere sees everything within me.
"I am never lost to him, nor is he ever lost to me"—
thus did that sage speak here and there, in the words of Arjuna and his teacher.
For if the self of consciousness were indeed severed from all objective entities, it would become a mere entity itself, like a jar or other things characterized by their own specific marks. ||911||
And for this reason, consciousness perishes by losing its nature as consciousness; for if that consciousness were to be cut off from its objects, it would indeed flee away.
Just as one’s own shadow follows one’s head, so too, when I tread upon my own feet,
the great multitude does not perceive anything that has been proclaimed by me.
Because it abides in the center of all, it is established within me;
likewise, because it is grounded in luminosity, this [consciousness] partakes in the state of non-existence.
The Sage declared that it is indeed destruction by way of both paths;
such is the sequence of things which is called the "envelope" (saṃpuṭa). 915.
Therefore, in the abode of the seat formed by the entire path, consciousness, having attained the state of being supported, returns once more to the state of being the support. (916)

And it is said in the *Anuttarayāga*: "Then, once again, there is the seat; however, for those wishing to enter here, [the procedure] follows the sequence of the formal request (*jñapti*)," so says the Sage. (917)
The Blessed One himself has declared that the universe is not otherwise than that [Self], for it is the freedom of non-dual consciousness that shines forth upon the path of duality. (918)
This distinction between the one who teaches and the one who is taught is established [only conventionally];
for one considers one's own self alone to be the supreme Lord Guru. (929)
One considers one's own uttered words to be the words of another; likewise, both the object to be established and that by which it is established [are considered as such]. (920)
For all that is indeed of the nature of the Self, yet it is conceived as distinct,
just like the state of being in a dream or the succession of oral instructions.
A dull-witted creature, hearing what is said by another, takes it to be for himself;
in the very same way, this entire worldly activity occurs while one is still in the womb of deep sleep.
If it is asked, "In that case, what would be the difference between dream and waking states?"—then [we reply]: has this not already been stated by the Lord in the *Svacchanda-tantra*? (923)
Thus, through the very sequence of formal declaration, there is a distinction between injunction and restatement;
yet "the Lord is everything" and "everything is the Lord" are indeed one and the same. 924.
In reality, like a jar or a pot, the universe is merely a modification;
"you alone are the denotable object of these"—thus did the illustrious Nārāyaṇa declare. (925)
But if there is no difference [between them], how can there be a distinction between injunction (vidhi) and restatement (anuvāda)? [The answer is:
"That which has protruding teeth is this Caitra"—here, the quality of having protruding teeth is first [stated as] the subject. (926)
If the portion "Caitra" is indeed restated [as a subject] and another [portion] is enjoined as distinct from Caitra, then how can that other [portion] be Caitra? (927)
In such cases as "The pot is Caitra," there would be no distinction between the positive injunction (*vidhi*) and the restatement (*anuvāda*);
therefore, the established position is that "Caitra" is one thing and "the one with protruding teeth" is another. (928)
The real injunction arising from mere cognition is employed for both injunctions and restatements toward those who have not yet grasped the meanings of the words and their positions; as in:
"This is a tree (pādapa)," [or] "This is a grower (bhūruha)."
Just as "kumbha" and "ghaṭa" are said to be synonymous, so too Maheśvara is said to be this entire world. ||929||
Thus, that state which is indeed complete through the yoga of the *saṃpuṭa* (the union of the two), within which hundreds of portions of dissolution and emanation remain contained; 930.
Some, with the desire to worship that very [deity] part by part, do so through [the divisions of] one and so forth, arising from doubling, such as four, six, twelve, and so on. ||931||
She divides herself through various sequences consisting of the wheels of consciousness;
that single consciousness is twofold, and as the essence of vision and action, it is threefold.
Furthermore, through the assistance of the power of unfolding (pronmeṣa-śakti), it is described as fourfold;
however, by virtue of the establishment of the bliss-nature of the power of consciousness (cicchakti), it is proclaimed as fivefold. ||933||
But through the investigation and deliberation upon the discourse of consciousness as expressed by the six vowels,
consciousness becomes twelvefold, having an identical range from the beginning of creation onwards.
Because each one consists of three aspects, or because of the fourfold nature within the triad,
consciousness impels emission and therein attains a state of redness.
It effects the destruction of stability and may give rise to doubt somewhere;
then, having withdrawn that portion of objective existence through its own power of reabsorption, [it manifests again]. ||936||
Within that [state], the nature of being the destroyer of merit and demerit is contemplated;
it does not desire either rapidity or cessation by virtue of its own sovereignty.
In this way, within herself, she who devours the circle of rays that constitute the factors of awakening withdraws the suns situated in the portions of the means of valid cognition. (938)
Then, having withdrawn the portion consisting of the imagined into the unimagined heart—which, though transcending all that, is the inner, undivided abode— [one should rest]. (949)
One should lead [the consciousness] through the gateway of the eyes as far as the universe, and then one should effect emanation; such is the application of the sequential order. ||940||
This wheel with twelve spokes revolves perpetually; for these [twelve months] constitute its gross form, consisting of the abundance of the lunar mansions, the zodiac signs, and so forth. //941//
By virtue of both the non-sequential and the sequential,
this wheel that has arisen unfolds in twos, threes, and in great numbers, through various sequential and non-sequential modes.
It devours the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, the act of knowing, and the knower. ||942||
Because it rests upon spokes that are like the infinite rays proceeding from this wheel,
the differentiation of wheels can never be counted.
For just as the white, yellow, red, and other colors on the feathers of a peacock appear here, flashing and flickering, even though they do not possess that nature [of being real]. (944)

Thus, the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśa), intensely filled with a subtle consciousness that is neither manifest nor dissolved, shines forth, variegated by the fluctuations of his states as they close and open. 945.
Through the closing of one [eye] and the opening of another, it revolves from the single-spoked wheel up to the thousand-spoked wheel in the blink of an eye.
Is it then an incalculable number, or perhaps one containing embryos mutually dependent upon each other?
Or is it not that wheel at all, but rather the single void itself that expands? 947.
That too shines forth either as containing within it infinite circles of existence, or as containing within it infinite space; it is called the single Great Space. ||948||
Just as the single sky alone shines forth in white, blue, and red,
and just as these clouds likewise appear again in many ways,
so too does the reality of consciousness manifest through forms devoid of calculation and enumeration.
It manifests independently through its own forms, yet none of those [forms] exist as such. ||949||
Thus my Lord, dwelling within my heart, himself explained this reality,
having assumed a manifold form.
Transmitted through the succession of the lineage of gurus. ||950||
Therefore, for those who are unable to attain firm conviction in this system,
does not the Lord [act] for the sake of awakening them?
He has taught various ways of arranging the mandala. ||951||
Just as a child is gradually associated with the various classes of letters through their respective conventions by means of lines,
so too [is one associated] with mudrās, maṇḍalas, mantras, and tantras.
When it is complete, it is joined to its own priceless abode.
Here too, something shines forth by His will alone,
possessing a gradation of being far removed or situated nearby; it may touch upon a portion or be established in the partless state.
Thus, there is indeed a manifold variety [of types] within the chapter on ritual action. ||953||
Thus, that reality which was indeed described as partaking in the nature of valid cognition is this very Goddess Parāparā, who shines forth in such and such ways. 954.

In this very context, that which is the supreme part (parāṃśa) is again the subjective part (mātraṃśa), while the other is the objective part (meyāṃśa); this has already been explained by us previously. (955)
Because even a minute portion exists in manifold ways within the supreme state,
the Supreme One, whose nature is that of the Lord of Mantras, is preeminent through the state of being both supreme and non-supreme.
But that in which the subsequent state (apara-bhāva) is predominant is called "mantra";
while that which is both supreme and non-supreme (parāpara), the Mother, is the one in whom the supreme and non-supreme are fully integrated.
He is called Vijñānākala, awakened by the supreme state;
through the conjunction with the predominance of the lower [state], he is indeed Pralayākala. (958)
Furthermore, that which is called the "entire" [reality] is indeed the Mother;
its state is manifold through the distinctions of the supreme, the non-supreme, and so forth. (959)
When analyzed, it produces an infinite number of varieties of Mothers;
however, seven varieties of Mothers are proclaimed as being primary.

It is indeed their own inherent powers that fall within the scope of the means of valid cognition; we consider that their very capacity for functional operation constitutes their nature as "powers. (961)
And that very state of being active is indeed instrumentality;
thus, through the distinction between the possessor of power and the power itself, there arise the knower, the means of knowledge, and the [resulting] cognition. (962)

The fourteenfold nature is declared to be the object of cognition (*prameya*), because the knower (*mātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*māna*), and the object of knowledge (*meya*) are proclaimed to be one. (963)
Then, from that [state], there is one consisting of fifteen, which is the single [principle] expanded by the prakṛtis;
even there, in each individual division, there exists that which has the nature of its own essential reality.
The infinite variety of divisions produced through both concise and detailed formulations is further extended by means of the sequence that synthesizes the divisions from water up to the root. (965)
The emergence of a vast proliferation of diversity arising from further divisions and subdivisions has been described in this way,
from the earth element up to the principle of *pradhāna*, as consisting of exactly fifteen types.
Up to the end of the *kalā* [tattva], the *sakala* [state] is the very nature of the Person (*pums*); it is neither the measurer (*mātṛ*) nor does it have the form of measurement (*māna*). ||966||
Therefore, the state of having thirteen aspects is established here;
at night, however, its essential nature is that of the *layākala*.
In the middle, on the other hand, it has the nature of the *vijñānākala*.
In the stage of knowledge (vidyāpada), there is the state of having the nature of the mantra. ||967||
In the Īśa [level], there is the state of the class of Mantreśvaras; then, in the auspicious abode (Suśiva), there is the culmination in its Lord.
Each preceding level therein manifests its own arrangement of the subject and the object of knowledge.
Therefore, the state of Śiva—non-dual with respect to any other perceiver, self-luminous, eternally one—shines forth.
From Mantreśa and Īśāna, there are divisions numbering thirty, seven, nine, and twenty-one. ||968||
And since power is not distinct from the possessor of power, it does not attain separation from him;
nor does power exist in the state of non-subjectivity.
Therefore, the essential nature is not endowed with power. ||969||
That light which shines forth through the non-differentiation of the principle of earth (dharātattva) is indeed Lord Śiva here; that supreme Brahman is the Earth. 970.

Those who, by the will of Śiva, impel those intent on bestowing the supernatural powers (siddhis) residing in the principle of earth (dharātattva) are the Great Lords of Mantra (mantramaheśvaras). ||971||
But the lords of mantras, being impelled, clearly manifest as the mantras that denote them;
having practiced the yoga pertaining to the earth-element through the knowledge of Śiva. (972)

But this is not the case for those who hold dualistic views, such as the Pāśupatas, Sāṃkhyas, Vaiṣṇavas, and others, who have not attained the eternal abode and who abide in the state of Vijñānākala. ||973||

Those who have reached dissolution at the end of a kalpa through the enjoyment of reality are like those situated in the state of deep sleep; here they are known as the "isolates of dissolution" (pralayakevalas). ||974||
Indeed, in deep sleep, the state of being dissolved into reality (tattva) is clearly perceived;
otherwise, how could there be such a fixed connection with dreams? (975)
Even the state of deep sleep appears variegated—clear, unclear, and so forth—since we observe a variety of recollections such as, "I slept happily," and the like. (976)

In this world, those individuals who have ascended to the earth and are defiled by impurities mixed with the unfolding of illusory karma are to be known as *sakala* (those with all [karmic fetters]). ||977||
The agitation that occurs when this very group of seven is engaged in its respective functions is what is called the "group of seven powers" (śaktisaptaka). Thus, [it is said]: 978.
Śiva is the nature of immutable consciousness; those three powers of his, however, assume the forms of the subject and the object by virtue of their own sovereignty. (979)

Because the aspect of the subject (grāhaka-bhāga) predominates and the aspect of the object (grāhya-bhāga) surges forth, that which is "seven times seven"—though appearing as a single, purely insentient entity characterized by the human nature—is [in fact the Self]. 980.
Its essential nature is thus established as threefold for each individual principle (tattva). Furthermore, when an object is to be grasped, there are sixteen moments (tuṭis).
Each is conceived as having an entry of two and a quarter finger-breadths;
among them, the first consists of the essence of the undivided flavor of supreme non-duality.
The final [moment], however, because of its identity with the object to be grasped, is not perceived separately; the penultimate [moment] is considered to be the grasper of its own nature. (983)

And therein, the first group of seven has attained a state free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpaka), being skilled in obscuring the shadows of the parts of conceptualization as they gradually emerge. (984)
They know that very form of Śiva to consist of the Supreme Power;
therein, the second group of seven consists of the state that is both supreme and non-supreme.
The distinction between "conceptual construction" and "recitation" appears [within consciousness];
thus, they are intent upon the mental formation within this subtle awareness. (986)
Whatever form they experience therein, what is the use of boastful talk?
For it is held that through the gradual reduction of differentiation, even the *tuṭis* [of time] come to an end.
Furthermore, the diminution of conceptual construction is the defining characteristic of non-conceptuality;
for it is like one who, having long been afflicted by suffering, subsequently attains a state of established happiness. (988)
Just as one forgets that suffering by way of resting in happiness, so too do people remain rooted in consciousness even when it has become free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa). 989.
By the power of the resting of conceptual construction, they do not take pride in that state;
through the gradual diminution of conceptualization, one proceeds toward the ultimate truth, which is devoid of conceptual construction.
Thus, let the one of keen intellect strive for focused attention thereon, so that the true nature of consciousness may be revealed. 990.

Attentiveness toward the relationship between the apprehended object and the apprehending subject—this is what is called [the state] therein, because it leads to the attainment of desired results. (991)
For this very reason, because of the great multiplicity of those [individuals], even the worlds attain diversity; thus, no transgression is admitted. ||992||
Prior to the corruption of time, this very sequence and non-sequence of time, as well as the ultimate reality of the directions, cannot be established by reason. (993)
For that [single entity] cannot produce the cognition of "prior" and "posterior" in such a way;
since there is no real object apart from the distinction of limiting conditions (upādhi), how could that [cognition] be imagined? //994//
For he who is superior in qualities to all others is therefore the Supreme Lord;
thus spoke He, who has fashioned the entire sphere of space and time from His own bliss.

Thus, for those who wish to enter into this manifold nature of reality, a threefold division has been described regarding the modes of immersion (samāveśa) due to the difference in their means. ||996||
This Śāmbhava means is non-instrumental (anupāya); beyond that is the Cid-upāya;
whereas the Āṇava means is insentient (jaḍopāya), and it is considered to be of many kinds.
Even though it is non-inert, there is an appearance of inertness due to the possession of the supreme Lord’s power;
therefore, the channels, the sense organs, and external objects serve as means for consciousness.
In that context, whatever apprehension of external forms occurs by relying on the activity of the senses is waking; it is vivid, stable, and recurs again and again. (999)
Dream is a construction produced by one's own mental constructs; it is the reverse of waking.
It is the experience of the *layākala* [state], which occurs due to the power of residual karma from dissolution, and not otherwise. (1000)
Due to the absence of night, he remains steady; while asleep, there is no experience of pleasure and so forth, because for the *jñānākala*, there is only pure enjoyment arising from impurity. (1001)
Those possessing differentiation—both the insentient and the sentient—are intended to be inherently distinct;
yet within that [state], the triad of the Mantra, its Lord, and the Supreme Lord reside in the Fourth state. ||1002||
To the extent that phenomena are capable of entering into the portion of Bhairava-consciousness, they themselves become non-dual, their individual essences dissolving away. (1003)
In the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), which consists of fifteen aspects, whatever appears clearly to anyone should be considered as their waking state. 1004.
That very same nature appears unstable; such is the dream state.
But when it appears indistinctly, even that which is right before one, that is the state of deep sleep. (1005)
That fourth state, which arises by virtue of which the synthesis of the triad occurs, should be understood as being like the thread of a garland, present within all distinctions. (1006)

"That which shines with the full weight of non-duality, in which all distinctions have been dissolved—that they call the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta); one should apply this [definition] everywhere. (1007)

For at the time of dissolution, one's own nature is the waking state, while that which precedes it is the dream state and so forth; thus, the wise person should follow this entire sequence everywhere. (1008)
Even when the Lord is fully present in one place alone, he is said to be beyond the fourth state (turyātīta).
Bliss is the fourth state (turya), while will itself is the seed-ground, which is the state of deep sleep (suṣuptatā).
Knowledge is the state of dreaming, while action is traditionally known as the waking state;
it is precisely here that the designations arising from the stages of yoga, such as "abiding in the body" (piṇḍasthatā) and so forth, are applied. 1010.
However, [the mandalas] beginning with Sarvatobhadra are fashioned by those possessing the knowledge of *prasaṃkhyāna*;
because the fourfold form exists within each one, they are therefore expanded. 1011.
In one place there is a fourfold form, then a triad, and then oneness; yet the Lord Bhairava is truly one, with the manifest form of the entire universe. (1012)
This entire path, beginning with Śiva and ending with the totality (sakala), is unified in its state of existence; it possesses a mode of being that is non-different from Bhairava. 1013.
Attaining autonomy through His own sovereignty, He manifests;
this very [reality], abiding in the nature of the subject, is conceived as the path of mantra (mantrādhvan). ||1014||
In its nature as valid cognition (*pramā*), this is defined as the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*);
having attained the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it proceeds to become the path of words (*padādhvan*). (1015)

Without abandoning its immersion in the nature of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa), it attains the state of being an object of knowledge (meyatā); thus, due to the absence of conceptual construction (saṃkalpanā), the path of the kalās (kalādhvan) is conjoined with the subject (mātṛ). 1016.
When the connection with the state of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*) is pure, let that be understood as the "path of reality" (*tattvādhvan*);
when there is a connection with its basis in grossness, it is described as the "path of worlds" (*bhuvanādhvan*). ||1017||

For when the state of the denotable object is swallowed by the reflective awareness of consciousness, it becomes intent on the protection [of the self] through the thought dependent upon the knowledge and action of Śiva. (1018)
Through the skillful intensity of his passion for the playful display of the entire multitude of powers, the path of mantra—which is essentially Śiva—arose suddenly and swiftly at the outset. (1019)
For the yogi who relishes the repose within pure, surging consciousness, his powers are unrestricted due to the capacity for all designations. ||1020||
Having been projected, their functions extend from their own selves up to the objects and the earth;
thus, within their own consciousness, they perceive as many objects within their own self.
Even children and animal subjects, who do not participate in linguistic convention, possess a true consciousness that reflects the nature of direct perception as they touch upon objects. (1022)

Relying upon this very [consciousness], which is the essence of uncreated mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) and which appears as various distinct cognitions according to each individual, they too attain a manifold state of subjectivity (*pramātṛtā*). (1023)
If conventions attain firm establishment within this consciousness of infinite, non-artificial colors, then even they come to function without being conventional. (1024)
But without this [ultimate convention], all the conventions established in many ways do not find rest in the mind, because they are joined with other conventions. (1025)
They would fall into the error of non-abiding because it would result in the destruction of the root [of cognition].
Furthermore, even in that case, how could a child be taught a convention? (1026)
Therefore, this infinite collection of phonemes belonging to Māyā, which is of such a nature, always unfolds while accompanied by the reflective awareness of consciousness (cid-vimarśa). ||1027||
And from that very [source], the illusory phonemes brought forth their production;
it is indeed determined that those non-illusory [phonemes] are their potency (vīrya). ||1028||
For instance, when the words of another are heard, the innate cognition of that dull-witted person is obscured; he does not attain the status of a knower regarding that object. (1029)
But for him whose dream enters into awakening while still containing within it differentiation, he attains the state of a subject within his own mass of illusory phonemes. (1030)
To the extent that this form transcends the uncreated, to that same extent a gradation of aesthetic wonder is conceived. ||1031||
But when that [insight] reaches a state of great intensity, those established in its very essence certainly attain a universal possession of poetic genius and eloquence. (1032)
For this very reason, when speech is perfected, the phonemes are to be fully cultivated; therefore, by that [perfection], they are spoken by one who is protected through being protected. (1033)
Then, until the Lord attains eternal rest, he simultaneously perceives many phonemes that are well-established as fulfilling various enjoyments.
At that very moment, having entered the ground of the object of knowledge, he becomes the first sprout within the mass of conventions regarding the nectar of saṃsāra. (1035)

In this way, it is certain that the state of being an object of knowledge, the nature of the knower, and likewise the state of being a means of knowledge, belong to the collection of thirty-six principles which constitute the Self. (1036)
In that regard, all this shines within the eternal Supreme Lord, in the form of a reflection and not as something external, because [it is so]. (1037)

Within the auspicious void of consciousness alone, such notions as "this body" and so forth appear as distinct to transmigrating beings, just as the notions of a snake and the like appear in a rope. (1038)
Since the doctrine of the death of a previous body belongs to the realm of dreams, what kind of birth of a new body could possibly follow from that death? (1039)
In a dream, however, because the mere generality of an intuition manifests by force, particulars appear; yet they are not even conceptualized in that way.

Just as certain *sāligrāma* stones possess hearts of variegated forms, so too does Consciousness, with its lines beginning from Māyā and ending at the Earth, possess a heart of variegated forms. (1041)
Cities, oceans, mountains, and so forth, conform to His will;
they do not themselves possess the nature of being causes or non-causes, nor of being existent or non-existent. (1042)
Whether the discipline has been long-established through its thorough eradication [of obstacles] and its continuous practice,
or even if it is not yet established, this Bhairava of the sky of consciousness remains independent.

In the circle of objective existence, the failure to reflect "I am thus" regarding that which partakes in non-difference from Bhairava— who is perfectly full as pure consciousness alone— is the cause of differentiation.
Just as no other agent is established by any means of valid cognition in a dream, so too should the creation be understood as belonging to self-cognition, which is independent. (1045)
For he who, while sporting in the variegated garden-city of the mind, realizes:
"I alone exist as the various states of being, which are composed solely of pure consciousness. (1046)
Thus, the various phenomena of birth and death—such as "I am born" and "I have died"—appear upon the wall of the mind, fashioned by itself, within that which is unborn and immortal. (1047)
The distinction between this world and the next consists merely in the consciousness of others;
however, the consciousness of a single moment of time remains undivided even when there is a difference in location. (1048)

If this creation had been material and not composed of consciousness, then why would even a single mountain have been perceived from within it? (Or, according to another reading: "Why would even a single mountain have spoken from within it?")

In the discussion regarding the relationship between the substratum and the superstratum among the categories beginning with the gross elements and the subtle elements, ultimately it is the power consisting of consciousness that is the sustainer, whose very nature is Śiva. (1050)
Therefore, it is cognition alone that acts in this manner; that cognition is Śiva.
Thus, within one's own self, that power is designated as the "common substratum" (sādhāra). 1051.
Even that which is purely volitional and without support does not fall downward, because it rests within the power of its own support; thus should the universe be contemplated. 1052.
The state of being earth and so forth belongs precisely to this deep-seated habituation (*rūḍhi*) such as "I am solid" (the reading is *ghana*);
until finally, at the end, the nature of Bhairava is realized as "I am consciousness. (1053)
Just as colors such as blue appear in a gem or a rainbow, so do they appear in Śiva;
yet in ultimate reality, these possess neither arising nor passing away.
To say that creation occurs only in this place or at this time is inconsistent;
for the creation of the Lord, whose nature is consciousness, extends even to space and time. (1055)
In the state of being intent upon wakefulness, within the range of three and a half cubits, distinct dreams occur during each watch, perceiving various directions and times. (1056)
For this very reason, we do not consider a so-called "moment" to be anything at all;
for even within a single moment of action, there exist many rapid activities. (1057)

Therefore, those who have attained the contraction of existence for even a moment— surely they, by means of this "night" (or, according to another reading, "this small vessel"), are adherents of the view of emptiness.
Therefore, he who is capable of making existent entities empty and likewise manifesting non-existent ones by virtue of his sovereignty is the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara). 1059.
Thus, the Supreme Lord is celebrated as having the universal form;
however, the existence of anything separate from Him, such as the earth and so forth, is not logically tenable.
And this has already been stated previously, so it will not be analyzed further;
moreover, the refutation of external objects has been extensively elaborated by many [authors]. (1061)
But if this is so, how can birth and death be the connection of the fruit of karma? Or has the previously mentioned sovereignty of consciousness been utterly forgotten? (1062)
For it is certain that this consciousness is independent; in whatever way it manifests, so does it truly appear, containing within itself all possible forms. (1063)
Just as sweetness exists in every atom of sugarcane in its entirety, so indeed does the state consisting of the entire creation exist within each individual atom. (1064)
But those scholars who dispute here, having failed to understand the root of reality, are surely intent on protecting their own mental empires. (1065)

The delusion that "this [world] exists" somewhere—in the vital breath, in space, in consciousness, or externally—arises from ignorance; it is manifested by the absence of sovereignty that emerges from the Lord's own necessity. (1066)
Therefore, the self-awareness of one's own consciousness appears here as the very nature of birth;
however, prior to that, consciousness does not possess its form as characterized by absolute sovereignty.
In this context, prior consciousness is designated as "past karma";
therefore, the consciousness that sublates that [prior] consciousness brings about the exhaustion of karma. (1068)
Just as that which was not done appears to me in a dream as "done by me," so too is the fruit of action seen [to arise] in the waking state; such is the nature of the matter.
And likewise, he in whom even a single consciousness arises that consists of the total incineration of the fruits of the mass of prior karma does not indeed partake of those fruits. (1070)
Furthermore, because it is intensely radiant with manifold cognitions, fame [arises] from fame;
it bears abundant fruit, like a seed watered by the waters of a celestial river. ||1071||
Thus, an action that has little fruit manifests when there is slight experience;
however, when it does not manifest, it is indeed fruitless—this is the principle regarding self-cognitions.

Even there, whatever smallness or greatness is attributed to cognitions, those [attributes] partake of that form through the ascension of the agent of action into the nature of cognition itself. (1073)
And that cognition which does not itself arise as containing such a result, nor likewise through association with a cognizer who apprehends another result; ||1074||
Even for another knower who experiences the fruit within consciousness, that [consciousness] is sufficient unto the end, regardless of the volitions and so forth of other knowers. (1075)
Awakened for the sake of protecting creation, he manifests the power of maintenance;
knowing all, he causes the conceptualizations that depend upon fruits to contract.
With the intention that "this creation consists of both fish-eaters and those who do not eat fish," the ancients instructed that one must perform service for others.
In this way, even for one who has died, such assistance is extended; furthermore, through the offering of funeral cakes and other rites, a reunion with a body is bestowed. (1078)
"May my own afflictions be better than causing suffering to others"—this is the conceived fruit of such difficult asceticism as his. (1079)
"Let living beings indeed accept that the prohibition against eating garlic and such things is declared by [the Buddha's] command to be entirely without reason. (1080)
Thus, in this determination of what is edible and what is inedible for swans, parrots, and others, a difference in cognition is appropriate; otherwise, it would not be possible in any way. (1081)
Thus, whether in the seen or the unseen, through the sequence of imagined parts and sub-parts,
that very same union of fruits is established today, rooted in the ground of consciousness.

The established rule is that in the world beyond, the body does not exist apart from the physical mass; otherwise, how could it be said that living beings who bear bodies are not mutually interconnected? ||1083||
By means of all those multitudes of scriptures, the stake of doubt was driven into the ground;
mounted upon the soil of the ignorant mind, it has reached the point of fruition.
"I have a provider of food today; thus, through the sequence of receiving alms, I have attained the fullness of my limbs, and with my body complete, I am well-established. (1085)
"By means of an unseen action (adṛṣṭa-kriyā) fashioned through [the roles of] son, disciple, or one's own self, I am a partaker of heaven, established in the ultimate enjoyment. (1086)
I have no one to give me alms, and I myself am a doer of great evil;
there is no protector for me anywhere—I fall into the ocean of hell. (1087)
"Sometime, somehow, there will be a savior for me"—such an expansive realization likewise bears fruit of its own accord. (1088)
Let there be no one to offer him funeral cakes or perform other rites;
nevertheless, he experiences that fruit which was fashioned by his own volition. ||1089||
But this intellect, firmly bound within by the cement of the thunderbolt of doubt, is consumed root and branch in an instant by the fire of Bhairava alone. (1090)
I am Śiva alone, the blazing fire that consumes the dream-palace of saṃsāra—which contains within it the entirety of diverse consciousness—shining forth with the realization: "I am Śiva. (1091)
Thus, that deluded one, whose consciousness has become variegated through the perception of karma,
falsely imagines the very process of volition to be a diverse cycle of existence.

Therefore, a child who dies devoid of other latent impressions (vāsanā) remains a child [in the next life], whereas one whose latent impressions of worldly existence (saṃsāra) are firmly established becomes [an adult]. ||1093||
Those [impressions] remain in that state until youth arrives again through the sequence of those very latent impressions (vāsanā). ||1094||
Through the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of [past] formations, a certain person conceives of various transmigrations;
yet, due to the impression of insentience, he becomes insentient himself, like wood driven by wind and air. (1095)
Through its conjunction with earth and water, it attains the nature of flower and fruit;
once consumed, it returns again to the state of the embryo in the form of semen.
As long as one repeatedly conceives of the various forms of saṃsāra,
Śiva remains fixed in one place alone, permeated by the latent impressions of his own habitual tendencies.
He experiences enjoyments fashioned by his own autonomy in celestial realms, hells, and other states;
sometimes these consist of earth, sometimes of water, and sometimes are a mixture of both. (1098)
Thus, this consciousness, which consists of the world, shines by its own nature;
wherever it is sustained, there itself pleasure and so forth arise from its own latent impressions.
He knows by means of another [cognition], yet he is not seen by that other; moreover, he perceives others in a different way.
In ultimate reality, neither space nor time exists at all.

For in the doctrine of difference (bheda-vāda), the state of being the whole or a part [of space] arises from the very locus of the limiting adjunct (upādhi); and the distinction of the locus itself is a distinction of the limiting adjunct. (1101)
Thus, by virtue of their mutual dependence, there is no spatial distinction whatsoever;
therefore, a difference in intrinsic nature alone is properly established as the basis for differentiation. (1102)
And it has been established that this [non-existence] does not apply to those whose sole nature is luminosity;
for they have been excluded by this very perspective of reflective awareness (parāmarśa). ||1103||

They, being filled with doubt due to the flood of suspicious scriptures and absorbed in them, [are deluded] by the conceptualizations of infinite insentient beings created within their own dreams. ||1104||
Those devoid of awakening are vainly seized by false doctrines and filled with doubt, just as consciousness, though long remained suppressed, awakens once again. (1105)
Nevertheless, it bears fruit through such means as the prescribed expiations (prāyaścitta) and so forth,
by one who possesses the sovereignty of freedom that manifests as this manifold appearance.

Whatever has been fashioned [as an object], that very thing assumes the form of a body and so forth, when it is joined with the appearance of error corrupted by the appearance of cold and the like. (1107)
Furthermore, when the channels and so forth are afflicted by contraction, expansion, or striking, and when the great mechanical bellows of the body—the wheel of vital winds—has gone astray; (1108)
By that [process], the vital breath (prāṇa) is dissolved, and the body becomes an insentient appearance;
this occurs either when he enters into a state of authority or through the sequence of prior latent impressions (vāsanā). ||1109||
In that very state, one may imagine an experience designated as the "other world," or else one perceives it as being like a stone, or again, one awakens.
And because it is commonly established that "this world is other," its status as belonging to the next world [is understood];
and whatever [such as heaven or liberation] is present in one's mind here according to common convention. (1111)
In that very same way, it appears externally; therefore, even therein, there is diversity:
bondage, liberation, happiness, heaven, suffering, and a state consisting of insentience. (1112)
Thus, consciousness alone, independent and of the nature of Śiva, shines forth;
for even when [an object] is further endowed with parts, the state of "I" remains exactly as it was. (1113)
Likewise, my state of being resides within the form of Bhairava, which consists of the universe;
even as a child, one perceives a Vetāla in the void as one who accomplishes real purposes.
The diversity of objects of meditation, worship, and so forth, thus produces purposeful action;
for one who is embodied and distinct [from the deity], having been summoned, instantly abandons his own enjoyments.
"O King, this report that 'he is coming' is fitting only as mere words;
however, all this [notion] of his having a formless nature and so forth is indeed logical. (1116)
For the Self itself, having become such, shines forth as such through differentiation;
this very nature belongs to consciousness, and it is that alone. (1117)
In the scripture, the impurity of action (kārma-mala) is defined by its being permeated by differentiation;
however, when engaged in rituals such as initiation, it does not extend the status of being an impurity.
For he indeed has undertaken the vow of burning away the entire transmigratory existence consisting of duality;
and initiation, in reality, is of that same nature, having the true consciousness as its essence. (1119)
Thus it has been stated in the Unsurpassed System (Anuttara-naya): "He who knows thus according to reality;
for when the sphere of duality has been stilled through such application of higher knowledge. (1120)
The Self alone is Śiva, the One; what is bondage, and what is liberation?
Nevertheless, this is being taught for the sake of entering the great consciousness of initiation.
This initiation, whose intrinsic nature is action, is for the sake of removing the impurities of karma and so forth;
it occurs when karmas have been projected by the power of necessity as determined by one's own nature.
Because his enjoyment is produced simultaneously through the power of mantra, so too are the determinations of space, the divisions of time, and the paths within the vital breath (prāṇa). 1123.
Its manifestations extend from the earth up to Śiva;
therein alone it becomes the locus for birth, enjoyment, authority, and dissolution. (1124)
Having been established, it is drawn upward from there and enjoined elsewhere;
thus, through the mutual union of the Guru, whose nature is rooted in certain consciousness, and the disciple.
Initiation, when performed by a mind free from ritual action, obstructs all the powers of prior karma.
Even there, the continuous sequence of rice, sesame, ghee, and sacrificial porridge, and so forth, was fashioned by the weight of the Śaiva doctrine of necessity;
yet even in that much, the expansion of night did not appear as a distinct entity.
Even though it has reached a state of being rootless, due to the activity of differentiation. ||1126||
Even though there is a distinction, this [state] is nevertheless the cause for destroying the merit and other factors that produce future existence in saṃsāra;
therefore, it is pure, and for that very reason, it is indeed the entire web of reality (tattvajāla).
Everything exists in only two ways: as pure or as otherwise.
Indeed, the pure [Self], inlaid with the three powers, shines as a couple (yāmala);
by that, this manifold expansion of the world-process (niyatiprapañca) is produced through the various operations of ritual action (kriyā), according to the arrangement of its functions.
The connection with such enjoyment is produced by something other than that which is extremely subtle. ||1128||
The assembly of mudrās and maṇḍalas, adorned with mantras and tantras, wherein all practices such as yoga become capable of bestowing the fruit. ||1129||
Firmly established in their desire for the attainment of the fruit of liberation, they regard here only uninterruptedness as the fruit itself. (1130)

For as long as there is no infinite delimitation, there can be no conception of sacrifice and the like; [this applies] even to an undelimited desire. Nevertheless, when the object known is the supremely beautiful non-dual reality, [it is so]. (1132)

Due to the sovereignty of the nature of consciousness, some may have a desire for specific fruits; with those very [fruits] as their aim, everything from the earth element upward is provided for their fulfillment. (1133)
The *Dhāraṇā-grantha* is said to consist of many divisions ending with Śiva;
for here, indeed, there is nothing that does not manifest as reality, as is the case in other systems.
Therefore, for those who abide in the foundation of truth, what could possibly fall into the realm of the rejectable? ||1134||
Thus, that reality which shines forth as the final subject of the seventeen chapters has been determined as the unsurpassed state of Śiva for those desiring its attainment;
and all this, including that which consists of opposing views, has been declared here in the *Jagadānanda*.
For it is because this entire phenomenal world exists here by having differentiation as its very life-breath. ||1135||
Thus ends the first section in the *Śrīmālinīvijayottaravārtika*, composed by the venerable Abhinavagupta, the most excellent teacher of the Great Mahāmaheśvara tradition. ||1||
Now begins the second section:
Thus the Lord Maheśvara exists as the self of the universe.
Through the practice of sequential knowledge and yoga, it is worshipped by means of the concentrations (dhāraṇās). ||1||
In the eighteenth chapter, the reality—which has transcended the net of duality, impurity, māyā, and so forth—is thoroughly elucidated. 2.
In that [state], practices such as breath control (prāṇāyāma) are described precisely as things to be abandoned;
for they possess no utility whatsoever as a means toward supreme realization.

How can that which is firmly rooted within internal consciousness be made to move outward into the body, the vital breath, and the intellect? Thus, let the sequence of practice through yoga be undertaken.
As for those who are striving to purify this consciousness by means of the path of practice—
We are in doubt as to what, where, from whence, and how they might act; for the reading here is "where, how indeed? [or "where, how?"]. 4.

For "practice" (abhyāsa) means repetition; and that [repetition] occurs through the differentiation of space and time, arising from the conjunction with either manifestation or its opposite, within the path of the body, mind, vital breath, and senses. 5.
Those who desire to enter the state of Bhairava, which is a single mass of light,
remain perfectly established simply by resting in consciousness that is once-and-for-all awakened.
Right hereafter, that limb which is beneficial to all is proclaimed;
for the concentrations (dhāraṇās) as well, when determined through that means, are of that same nature. (7)
Indeed, when there is no firm foundation, what confidence can be placed in reasoning? Or is it that your own words are not likewise struck down by such lack of foundation? (8)
For how can those who have determined that scripture alone is the sole means of valid cognition reach a certainty when there exists a multitude of scriptures contradicting it? (9)
In that case, the renown of the great multitude is the cause of its authority;
its lack of foundation [is established] because there is the possibility of a great multitude who contradict it. (10)
Even perception, when directed toward desire and the like, is indeed a vessel for an infinite regress of subsequent cognitions, once the awareness of a subverting factor has been observed.
If even one's own self-awareness is sublated therein, how indeed could that which is skilled in joining distinctions produce the world of conventional practice? ||12||
But for us, there is no non-abiding anywhere at any time;
for those [for whom], the supreme ocean of Bhairava is everywhere complete.
In particular, it is with respect to those very people that reasoning lacks a firm foundation—those who have attained the supreme nectar of consciousness by crossing the ocean of reasoning. (14)
For indeed, all branches of logic, failing to touch upon self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*), have nowhere attained the auspicious ultimate fruit. (15)
For the entire meaning of the scriptures has non-duality as its essence for the sake of attaining that [reality];
those of deluded intellect take delight in the distinctions that have been elaborated therein. (16)
And logic (*tarka*) is characterized by differentiation; it is solely skilled in cutting away arguments. [Objection:
But surely, even in the case of non-duality, there is some utility for logic. (17)
And even that [duality] is not at all inconsistent with the vision of supreme non-duality;
for this very reason, supreme non-duality consists in the grace of the entire universe. (18)
He declares the supreme means for that to be the Heart, whose nature is vibration;
that which, within the Heart, consists of pure consciousness.
One's own self-reflection is the wonder of the full consciousness;
it suddenly and forcefully [the reading "haṭha eva sa" is also found] causes the manifestation of the universe to dissolve [the reading "malinīkṛta" is also found]. ||19||

He is filled with the perfect bliss that shines forth from the two states— beginning with the grasping at existence and ending with the non-final [state] (the reading *bālagraha* is also found)— and he consists of the joy of the entire world.

To the extent that this entire universe, which is clearly the throbbing of the Heart— the abode of emission—

By that much, it enters here into the power of the Trika.

This entire universe, whose nature is consciousness, flashes forth within the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self;
it then rests upon the trident of the three powers.
By way of the path of emission belonging to the Śāmbhava level. ||23||
That which is thus chanted as "Sat" is this very fullness here, whose nature is the "I," the heart where Śiva and Śakti are united.
Only that which is of the nature of vibration (sphuraṇa) always manifests. ||24||
Here, the sequences of creation, dissolution, and maintenance manifest perpetually through the eternal Self, by the hundreds, even by the thousands of millions.
Accumulated by Hara, Viṣṇu, and the Lotus-born (Brahmā). ||25||
But here, for one who is unable to enter immediately through the previously mentioned collection of methods,
the vibration of the Heart is revealed by way of the Śākta means [the reading "in sequence" (krameṇa) is also found]. ||26||

Having gained access to the path of the heart through the impulse of the vital breath at the tip of the trident, he is intent upon resting in the digit of the moon of consciousness situated within it. ||27||

Then, instantly abandoning that ground and casting off those states beginning with "joyless" (nirānanda) which are situated within the midst of the five elements [the reading being *tryaramadhye*], ||28||
One should abandon the former stage and proceed to the latter, being intent on perfect rest;
for from that arises the ground consisting of innate bliss, which follows upon the state of peace.
The two, devoid of worldly joy yet possessing supreme bliss, are united with the Puruṣa;

A certain state of great bliss, characterized by the left-hand path (vāmācārā), shall shine forth as consciousness within the great abode of Bhairava, wherein all consciousness is assimilated. (31)
Great bliss, having become the bliss of consciousness, proceeds again and again;

In the Trika, which consists of the synthesis of duality and non-duality through its universal nature, [the deities] are either non-different, or different, or even both different and non-different. ||33||
When the states of one's own bliss and so forth are joined with the fivefold state of bliss, they become possessed of the exuberant state of the bliss of the universe. ||34||
Intrinsic bliss (nijānanda) is based solely on resting in the aspect of the subject;
whereas the state consisting of the absence of bliss (nirānandātmikā) arises from resting in mere emptiness (śūnyatāmātra). ||35||

When there is a resting upon the state of the object of knowledge, supreme bliss arises fully; yet when the object is entirely filled by the convergence of infinite objects of knowledge, [that bliss is likewise present]. (36)
Because it is the union with the relish [of consciousness] through the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is established as "Great Bliss" (*mahānanda*).
The knower (*pramātṛ*)—who is skilled in swallowing the entire process of the flux of means and objects of knowledge—is the one who knows all. [The reading is *pramātā sarvam eti*.
When one attains a rest that is perfectly full and free from all limiting conditions, then indeed there is the bliss of consciousness, which is not augmented by anything insentient. ||38||
And there is no fixed abode whatsoever that is differentiated or insentient in nature;

"That which is unappropriated consciousness, nourished by the supreme nectar—that alone is the abode of the bliss of the universe; so our Guru has declared. (40)

The ground of the palace is sprinkled with water dripping from the lotus-creepers hanging from the balconies;

By means of the unsurpassed nature, which proceeds through the activity of speech, and which possesses the yoga of the emergence from the dissolution of the supreme egoity that is the reflective awareness of consciousness. ||44||

When the objective reality is illuminated by the sun—which consists of twelve digits and is emptied by the power of exertion—and when it is filled and thoroughly contemplated, [it becomes manifest]. 45.
By the power of being slowed down by that swallowing, [the breath], having entered the fire of awakening and properly emitting the *kalās*, partakes of the sixteen-fold *kalā*.

By the heart-born [wisdom] arising from the absence of investigation into the substantiality of entities, and by resting upon the Kulanetrī who is the immediate yoga of external procreation; ||48||
One should always abide in that which is eternally established through the state of the *Rudrayāmala*,
[perceiving] that garland of steps of power within the body, senses, qualities, and vital breath.

Having ascended the ground of the trident, which is all-pervading, the supreme life-sustaining digit, and which is joined with the three channels (nāḍīs), [one attains liberation]. ||51||

[One should contemplate] the series of steps consisting of the eyebrow, the point, the end of sound, and power, which are respectively expanded, contracted, and finally attained as a state of oneness.

She whose abode is the emission of the great root-piercing spike unified [with all things],

This [speech], which has acquired a supreme designation through its skill in fulfilling all [needs], is devoid of beginning and end, and is characterized by its inclination toward the universe.

Having attained the Goddess—the moonlight of the consciousness-moon in the sky of the heart, who presides over the triad—what indeed does one not obtain, and what does she not cause one to attain? (56)
Therefore, in this case, while the Supreme exists, when the yogi desires to enter therein by means of the methods pertaining to the body of meditation, he trembles for that long.

One should first enter into the perfect conscious self, which is free from the illusion of duality, by means of the gradual process of ascending through one's own power. 59.
Today, that sleep of his— which brings about the loosening of the body's immersion— would still be of a trembling nature,

This is the unmanifest sign (liṅga), consisting of the nature of Man, Śakti, and Śiva,

With all mental fluctuations dissolved through the union of the Great Thousandfold World-system, his mind became completely filled by the massed multitude of his own radiant rays. ||86||

When the yogi slightly expands the aperture of consciousness, all the channels of the senses within [the body] become the locus for the traversal of the cakras. 95.

With his entire being sealed by the mudrā that bestows immediate experience, he is the vigilant Bhairava, the manifest form of consciousness who is the presiding lord of all. 98.
That yogi, filled with wonder, attains the self-awareness of his own nature—a state that remains unshakable even amidst the arising and passing away of various perceived objects. (99)
The water situated in a pond does not flow elsewhere;

Thus, consciousness itself, unfolding spontaneously through the impetuosity of its own radiance,

For that [impurity] cannot exist rootless in one who has ascended by a mere opening of the eyes;

In this way, one surely delivers oneself from the domain of the ocean of duality, even while this mind is submerged in the flavor of sense objects. (108)
Those who restrain their own path of the mind, like that of a horse, do not become inwardly moistened, just as a water-tight gourd does not absorb moisture. (109)
Because it is impossible for those [faults] to be refuted, their minds run along millions of wrong paths;
thus, their minds generally long even for suffering, wondering, "What might this be? (110)
One may become detached even from pleasure through knowledge [realizing] "this is that";
for thus has the Guru instructed in many ways in his own teaching. (111)
The functions of the senses subside only through disregard and detachment;

With their doubts dissolved regarding objects, the means of enjoying them, and the resulting pain or pleasure,
they remain unmoved even while their minds are deeply immersed [in the world].

while the internal organ likewise renders assistance to it,

The yogi may arise, traversing various paths of worldly activity, yet shining with the potency of mantra. ||118||

The method for attaining what has not yet been seen is manifold. ||119||
Therefore, this [view] is without means, because of the lack of connection between the means and the goal;

Even though this [ultimate reality] is beyond all means, because it possesses some slight connection [to them], this teaching regarding the means has been set forth in many ways in this scripture. (121)
Just as children are clearly introduced to the truth regarding the nature of letters through written characters, so too are the deluded led step by step by various appropriate means. (122)
And for that very purpose, even regarding the non-dual supreme reality, some appropriate forms of worship, meditation, and so forth, are respectfully described in this scripture. (123)
Whatever gladdens the mind, regardless of where the senses may be situated,
should be joined within the abode of the true Brahman, which is consciousness, in the self that is the aperture of Brahman.
By relying on the state of immersion in the true existence that follows the Self, in the sequence of worshiping the various wheels of powers belonging to the supreme lords of the Kula. 125.
By its very nature, it effortlessly attains the state of being an instrument;
having made the earth its support, which has been purified by the sprinkling of the essence of wonder,
