But for him whose mental activity is fully awakened consciousness and who desires no fruit whatsoever, meditation on the universal form unfolds at all times. (138)
For a Kulayogin who is reeling from the intoxicating liquor of the overflowing essence of Bhairava, whatever arises does so in whatever manner. (139)
In the Northern tradition, the mudrā is defined as the penetration into the body, consisting of exhilaration and melting; it is the seal that has taken possession of the entire world. (140)
This particular method of yoga resides in the heart of someone or other, for whom the wheel of consciousness quickly becomes gracious, provided they are not of their final birth. (141)
Even while being observed by the world and remaining within the constraints of the body,
one attains an indescribable consciousness in an instant through yoga that has taken root.
In this very matter, however, the wisdom of our former noble teachers is most profound.
He perceived the absence of the delusions of worldly existence. ||143||

It is sufficient [to rely] on the Vedas, Sāṃkhya, Bhedavāda, Nyāya, the teachings of the Sugata, worldly sciences, the Pañcarātra, the ritual scriptures (kriyāśāstra), the established doctrines (siddhānta), and so forth. ||144||

By all those who, through their respective applications of propriety, have ascended to their own specific modes of activity while cultivating the portions of knowledge and action that are appropriate and fitting. ||145||

For one who is established here [in this state], no purification whatsoever is required anywhere;

Furthermore, it is clear that a defect (mala), being non-pervasive, cannot be an obstructor of that which is all-pervasive.
One should likewise establish the non-emptiness of the space within the jar by way of its own nature.

If, because the self is the subject of authority, impurity does not produce any effect [upon it], how could it be capable of obscuring it? Or rather, my dear sir, what is the point of this question? 169.
Indeed, the mere existence of impurity is called its obscuration;
the soul is described as being "obscured" when it is accompanied by impurity. (170)
Indeed, by this same principle, even for those liberated souls who have attained Śiva-hood, a real obscuration persists solely due to the continued existence of impurity (mala). (171)
Furthermore, when the self is obscured by impurity, does it not even perceive that very impurity? If it does not perceive it, what other impurity can be said to exist for it? (172)
Indeed, what impurity could there be from this? For then, even without the powers of knowledge (*vidyākalā*), omniscience would arise; and that impurity must already be known. (173)
Having abandoned those various diverse means devised by oneself, whatever obscuration may exist within one's own self, [one should abandon that] by means of this [teaching]. //174//
How will the states of being a knower and an agent belong to this [Self] in respect to jars and other objects? [Objection:
But surely, limited knowledge and agency are taught as being [the functions of] *vidyā* and *kalā*. (175)
In this way, those of deluded minds are deceived, but not the wise;
for this illusion is of a dull nature, as are its products, such as the *kalās* and so forth. (176)
How could that whose nature is acid be capable of manifesting consciousness?
And once consciousness is manifested, how could it be characterized by such attributes as "limitedness" (kiṃcit-tva) and so forth, given that it is all-pervading (vibhvī)? ||177||
How indeed could it be specified? For that [specification] is appropriate only for an object consisting of parts.
But surely the Lord, having *kalā* and *vidyā* as his instruments, would manifest consciousness (*citta*). (178)
Let it be clarified from all sides: alas, there can be neither incapacity nor lack of apprehension [on the part of the Self].
And while this impurity is eternal, how will liberation ever come about for it? (179)
"The power of Rudrī belongs to impurity, and it either ceases somewhere or proceeds somewhere"—fie on this talk of the deluded! (180)
What kind of synthesis could there be for insentient things? Without that [synthesis], how could this [world] come to be?
If, on the other hand, it is admitted that even in that case the Lord is the cause, [then our position is established]. (181)
For what reason would that deity set that power into motion, and once it has been set in motion, for what reason indeed would he cause it to cease again? (182)
If it is argued that [the soul acts] out of its own autonomy, why is that very [autonomy] not accepted as being complete?
Furthermore, there is no such thing as a "digestion" (pāka) of impurity, which is of the nature of darkness. 183.
For by means of the application of identity with another, it destroys that [object's] stable nature;
by this same process, impelled by the will of the Lord, [the agent acts] due to the connection with impurity (mala). (184)
"That which is said—that a beast, possessed by talk of greed for enjoyments, is favored by creation—is fundamentally flawed; therefore, it is produced from that [ignorance]. (185)
They know that impurity (mala) is nothing more than the mere play of concealing one's own nature;
for how could the independent, all-pervasive Lord not manifest something within Himself? (186)
Furthermore, that which is claimed to be karma must first be examined;
for even if a connection with karma were established, how could such a thing [as this] be possible? (187)
How could there be what is called the great dissolution or the great creation?
Surely, in that state, karma is brought to a standstill by the will of the Lord. (188)

Whether through the conjunction of indifference toward action or by depending on another action, does God [act] or not? In the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), there is indeed the possibility [of His acting]. (189)
In the absence of such [a creator], in what part could he possibly attain sovereignty?
All this, including creation, dissolution, and so forth, must arise from karma alone. (190)
Alternatively, if the Lord were independent of karma, then he, being omnipresent, would always perform actions whose effects are already obstructed by [prior] karmas. (191)
Is it not the case that their very nature consists in the production of experience?
How could this be their nature if it has come about through external conditions? (192)
For the intrinsic nature of entities is independent; therefore, that which is the form of actions when they are independent of a Lord or a desire is their own essential body. (193)

Furthermore, what purpose does the Lord serve in awakening even those karmas that remain dissolved during the dissolution? For what indeed could be accomplished by them once they have been seen [again]? (194)
If he too has been driven far away for the sake of purifying the impurity, then since this self is indeed all-pervading, what indeed can it do? (195)
Thus, the prior investigation has been explained in detail:
the intelligent Lord stands as the maker in relation to the clay, the staff, the wheel, and the string. (196)
In what respect, then, does the potter’s agency reside?
[It resides] in the sprouting, the production of fruit, and so forth, of seeds that ripen without being ploughed. (197)
What logic is there in saying that [the self] previously acted as a cause for crops but not for [other] things?
This is "bad karma" and this is "good karma," distinguished by their different fruits. (198)
Thus, regarding that which has been differentiated, what else could it be there but the unfolding of his own will? If he is independent, why does he inflict such suffering upon himself? (199)
He who, ever filled with the essence of compassion, constantly accepts [the suffering of others], surely acts in such a way by his very nature; therefore, this action yields its fruit. (200)
Reflecting that [the soul] may be pacified by performing expiatory rites and the like, the Lord likewise composes the scripture which provides diverse instructions. (201)
What logic is there in saying that such is the very nature of these actions?
One like me holds that the seed has the inherent nature of producing a sprout. (202)
They are capable of understanding [the meaning] through the linguistic usage of the ancient sages;
however, the Lord (Īśvara) never [acts] without his own will.
Having observed the skillful variety of the fruits of karma,
if the Lord were therefore the creator of all things,
then one's own group of selves could not possibly be the agents.
If even they are not agents,
then God is not the agent of all with respect to these who are devoid of karma.
And thus, this so-called "action" is not tenable when viewed through the lens of dualistic perception;
this much is the summary here, while the detailed exposition has been shown elsewhere. (205)
O God, He is indeed one, whose essence is consciousness; therefore, by His own nature, He is the creator of all.
Because of His manifold variety, He is called the "Yogi of Karma. ||206||
And if that which is known as Māyā, established as the cause of the universe, were clearly eternal and containing within it the portions of all principles down to the earth, [then... 207.
Dissolution could never occur, for it would [otherwise] exist as a manifest state— [or rather, according to another reading, "because of the absence of manifestation"]—
since we do not recognize what so-called "manifestation" is, given that it is cognition which constitutes the state of being apprehended. (208)
The state of being apprehended by the supreme knowledge of God exists eternally;
if that [state] were non-existent, how could God be the cause? (209)
Just as one clearly fashions a jar, so it will be with the Lord;
yet this is not so, because of the distinction between internal and external forms and instruments. (210)
It is logical that there should be cognitions ranging from clear to unclear in the case of a potter; however, this is not so for the Lord, who possesses clear and sublime prior cognitions. (211)
In which case would a portion not be known, even where there is a dependence on a manifest individual?
For those who maintain the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavādins), it is clearly established that [the effect] resides even in the cause and its location. (212)
Furthermore, it would clearly be inconsistent to say that "the universe" is within Māyā;
for the pervasive Śivas and their selves are mutually identical with the constituent principles (tattvas). (213)
And how indeed could there be [degrees of] manifestation, given that [consciousness] is obscured by its own pervasiveness?
The supreme expansion of consciousness is called its differentiation. (214)
The multitude of illusory coverings, as well as the collection of instruments, has already been examined; and the category of effects has likewise been discussed. ||215||
As long as the universe does not manifest—devoid of any superimposition upon the state of Śiva—it should be understood that this is merely a discourse on [the Lord's] sovereignty. 216.
Thus, in the absence of impurity and the like, what would initiation be, who indeed would be the initiator, and who could be the recipient of initiation? Nothing at all would be tenable. (217)

How could the placement (nyāsa) performed upon the entire path—consisting of the disciple, the path, the fire, the jar, the mandala, the ladle, the sacrificial grass, and so forth—possibly be accomplished? 218.
Indeed, they would not be merely that many, for surely [they arise] by the power of mental construction (saṃkalpanā);
for surely this entire relationship between the object of purification and the purifier has been proclaimed. 219.

If that which is imagined were to bear fruit in reality, then those who have acquired the splendors of their kingdom through the power of their imagination would triumph, owing to the attainment of rest in the sovereignty of heaven. (220)
How is it that entities existing within the path of powerful conceptualizations of form do not bear fruit accordingly, just as [the power of] meditation and so forth destroys poison? (221)
Meditation tainted by doubt is merely the firmness of one's conceptual resolve;
such meditation will not bear fruit, for it does not grasp either of the two sides.
Alas! If that fruit were to arise from the application of mere conceptualization, then what external objects, devoid of consciousness, do you desire? (223)
By mere intention alone, the consecration pertaining to the sacrificial pit, the fire, the guru, and the disciple is accomplished;
that very [intention] appears as the fruit, and only its consciousness remains.
And the manifestation of such a form by independent consciousness is indeed to be understood as initiation (dīkṣā), by which living beings are liberated. 225.

For this very reason, regarding the essential nature, the grasping, or the measurement of sesame seeds, clarified butter, and so forth, no specific sequence or restrictive rule has been prescribed here in the scripture. (226)
Now, is there not indeed a rule among the mantras that pertains to all castes?
For the supreme form has been described [as such]; why then is initiation not likewise [universal]? 227.
In this very way, what is considered beneficial for one who is burning with passion?
However, it is certainly [beneficial] for those who have not yet attained firm rootedness in that [state]. (228)
This rule regarding mantra has been proclaimed so that it may become effective;
for those mantras are awakened when they abide on the path of reflective discernment (vimarśa). 229.
By virtue of their own freedom, the mantras—which consist of the agency of the self-sufficient abode of consciousness—indeed enter that teacher through the application of identity. (230)
Even the instruments, when made independent, attain the status of agents;
in this same way, whatever other procedures are considered for rites such as initiation [attain agency]. (231)
What indeed is the duty for those performing [actions], and how is there even a prohibition? Those [objections] are also applicable here; all of that has been established in this very [work]. (232)

And all of this has been clearly refuted in that very [work], since its negation has already been demonstrated; furthermore, why would one who has taken to the path of non-duality [engage in such arguments]? (233)
Even that which was enjoined is prohibited, and even that prohibition is itself negated;
in this way, this ocean of self-awareness surges forth within its own self.
And thus, this entire universe, beautiful with the bliss of the Self, utterly destroys its opposite—the aspect of duality—in this very manner. (235)
By that much, the excellent rays [of wisdom], radiant with the weight of their own luster, emanate from all sides from the moon of knowledge born from the mouth of the Supreme Lord. (236)
Dissolved by the mere falling of the mass of rays from the moon of Śiva, the Kālakūṭa poison, which [otherwise] consists of all the cool-rayed [moons of worldly existence], acts as an elixir. (237)
There, plunging incessantly and reeling from drinking its essence, we remain transformed into that very essence—pure and liberated from the threefold suffering. (238)
The power of the Supreme Lord is said to be his will; indeed, having arisen from him,
it attains a state distinct from Īśvara and the other [categories].
The functioning of the power of the moon of the abiding consciousness. ||239||
That mass of rays which, it is said, issued forth from all sides of that moon in its fullness—
this indeed is what is described as having the nature of action.
The innate power of the Supreme Lord is identical with the universe. ||240||
This very Supreme Bhairava, overflowing with the power of the Triad, unfolds;
nothing else exists apart from Him.
His victory is proclaimed as his own self-manifestation. ||241||
For that very reason, it is logical for us that these conquerors of the world possess a manifest meaning, even though it is already evident;
such is the nature of the connection with many denotations.
The fullness of that consists in the differentiation of its statements. ||242||
Thus, this single verse alone clearly explains Bhairava himself, the conscious self, who is filled with the entire array of all states of being. (243)
Those whose vision is presided over by Garuḍa for the sake of destroying the poison of saṃsāra, and who consume only the nectar of the universe (Viṣṇu), attain the state of immortality. 244.
Thus it has been shown that by means of its own self-luminous self-awareness, this much is established;
apart from that, nothing at all can be conceived. (245)
Indeed, that alone is truly real which rests within one's own self-awareness;
for truthfulness could never exist in anything that depends upon another point in time.
The connection of consciousness with time has been refuted in detail;
therefore, it exists by extending through space according to its own self-awareness.
Likewise, that which has been placed upon the touchstone of valid cognition does not lead to doubt; for it is stated in the treatise that such a thing is not non-existent. (248)
That which does not ascend to one's own self-awareness is no different from mere prattle; that is the scripture, and that is the systematic exposition, which unfolds within self-awareness. (249)

All these arisings and perishings of the entire world are born from the Heart, just as [the dream state] arises from that which is called deep sleep; this is established by one's own consciousness through the study of the scriptures. (250)

The collection of form, light, and mental attention constitutes withdrawal; their persistence is maintenance; their emission is creation; and for the wise, the closing and opening of the eyes is the conceptualization of contraction. (251)
Thus, this state consisting of the knower, the known, and the means of knowledge is always the self-constructed manifestation of one's own perfectly full consciousness. (252)
For she herself is indeed the self-nature of all things, in all directions, locations, times, and forms;
for it is from her alone that the determination of truth and falsehood arises. (253)
The teacher Utpaladeva has also taught this very point:
"My own perception, though externally consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, [is established] within its own consciousness. (254)
"Let him see"—this is the sovereign constraint of the independent [Lord], designated as the senses;
it alone, having become established from Śiva down to a worm, rests upon its own consciousness. (255)
That very [reality] is Saṃsāra in the divine state; that is Śiva, the Supreme Lord.
One who has attained rest therein is designated as "liberated. (256)
By the grace of this [consciousness], all beings from Brahmā down to the immovable [plants] live;
let it be understood that this consciousness is eternally unimpaired. (257)
For that goddess shines even when she is not accompanied by him;
in some places she establishes herself, while in others she brings about corruption. (258)
The Supreme Goddess, though barren of any distinction between proof and refutation, establishes things in one way and yet does not undergo transformation. (259)
And it shines as suchness, for she is indeed independent and manifest;
he is the glorious Lord Maheśvara, who is the teacher even of the ancients. (260)
Out of a desire to favor the world, he spoke thus:
"O fools, why do you remain thus in vain, clinging to words that are essence-less and like the cawing of crows, thereby obscuring your own true consciousness?"

Whatever is commanded by the deity of consciousness— even if it is not commanded— everyone who honors that in its proximity becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta) in that respective place. ||261||
Therefore, in this system of policy, consciousness itself is called the Guru, because it swallows the entire universe through the process of emanation and reabsorption. (262)
In this context, that which is the primary conventional usage is called the "supreme connection.
Whatever knowledge is imparted by means of this [connection] is indeed *sāṃsiddhika* (innate). ||263||
Where the eternal abode of our lineage of gurus resides, from which the various branches of the Traiyambaka and other lineages proceed. (264)

Where it was previously stated that the identity with ignorance perishes, this [identity] nevertheless appears because self-awareness, while grasping its own manifold variety, manifests it as such. ||265||
The encounter with the scriptures— whether concerning the intermediate state, the Great One, the divine, or the non-divine—
is like the reality itself; it consists of the rays of one's own speech fashioned by the Guru,
wherein the preeminence of one's own self-awareness is made manifest.
Indeed, based on the teacher, the scriptures, and oneself, this effort has been primarily undertaken for that purpose. ||267||
The Guru is dependent upon the scriptures and their commentaries, yet he is established in the self-awareness of his own nature;
therefore, all this [is known] through that self-awareness.
Success is attained; indeed, it never reaches a state of being unbearable. ||268||
O you who seek liberation, let this scripture be investigated with diligent effort;
do not let your life be wasted by being spent on other treatises. (269)
Whether it be any view of non-difference or even a view of difference, it finds its fulfillment in this very [reality] alone; therefore, let this be investigated. (270)
Just as one who has fully understood [the nature of] the time of dreaming [perceives it] accordingly, so too is one whose heart is always awakened by the constant practice of this treatise. 271.
That scripture is nothing but one's own self-awareness, and that [awareness] is devoid of dependence;
if it were described in such a way, then let its validity be said to be intrinsic. (272)
That which is indeed the teaching, the object to be taught, and the teacher—therein it is untainted by time, beautiful in its non-dual sovereignty. (273)
Incorporating that state of his own as something inseparable, the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha spoke [of it] in the venerable Kiraṇa scripture. (274)
All of this is for the sake of engaging [the audience], yet due to the diversity of listeners,
this distinction is conceptually constructed through metaphorical designation based on a difference in meaning.
No distinction in the fruit should be imagined here; if one were to imagine such a distinction, it would be incorrect.
This [power] of the Lord is divided into ten, eighteen, eight, and eight varieties. (276)

For the individual soul who is eager to attain that [state], which has as its sole fruit the acquisition of the true being of Śiva, there is eligibility [only] because of the disregard for caste, family, social class, and so forth. (270)
As long as a single unified discourse proceeds once it has begun,
the wise recognize this as one [work], despite the variety arising from the relationship between primary and subordinate elements.
Likewise, the Trika scripture, the teacher who is non-dual in nature, the collection of subsequent fragments of speech, and the treatises [are all one]. (279)
And although the various occurrences of illusory duality manifest clearly, nevertheless, the attainment of Śiva remains the primary fruit at the end. ||280||
And there is indeed only one qualified person who is the recipient of the attainment of the state of Śiva;
nevertheless, when that much alone has occurred within the context of this treatise, [the goal is achieved]. (281)

Whatever result is clear, primary, or the ultimate result (*paryantaphala*)— whether it be the principal factor (*aṅgin*), its constituent part (*aṅga*), its opposite (*vipakṣa*), another position (*parapakṣa*), or something else— [is to be understood accordingly]. (282)

Moreover, such a person is a vessel for the manifestation of the various factors that counteract those [faults], provided they possess a body and so forth that are suitable, and share in the refinement [of their faculties]. (283)

Such a procedure for the ritual empowerment has been prescribed for both the guru and the disciple; likewise, one who has resorted to the elixir (rasāyana) that destroys death [is also qualified]. (284)

Previously, for the sake of attaining refinement, there was that transformation brought about by decoctions, emetics, purgatives, and initiation; however, it does not apply to the ritual procedure hereafter.
Therefore, the restriction of authority arises from the command of that body and so forth;
for this reason, it is said that the Vaiṣṇavas and others are dependent upon the teachings for bound souls (paśu). ||286||
They are not authorized in the Śaiva Tantra, nor are they Śaivas in the Vāma sphere;
they are not even in the Dakṣiṇa, nor would they be in the Kula doctrine or the Trika. (287)

It is stated in the Śrībhairavakula that a guru who is fit for the performance of the fivefold initiation is one who has transcended the lower currents or one who is established in the Trika scriptures. (288)
In this way, there is a single authority based on the foundation of the reality of the Self;
however, due to the distinction in the substrata of the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*), there is a diversity of authorities.
In the Svacchandatantra it is stated that Śiva is the fruit in every scripture, because all things originate from Śiva and thus have the state of Śiva as their fruit. (290)

And in that very same place, moreover, it is stated in the *Ūrdhvatattvavivecanā*: "That which has not been taught by the Sāṃkhyas, nor by the lords of Yogins, nor, O Dear One, by the Pāñcarātrikas... (291).
And so on, up to the three hundred and sixty-three [objections] raised by the disputants; for they are capable of discerning only that much. (292)
How could they be of the nature of those who know the reality of Śiva as undifferentiated?
Or rather, even in that case, they possess only a partial existence of Śiva. (293)
In that case, there would certainly be no clear logical connection;
for in a sentence such as "Devadatta" and so forth, the analysis (vigraha) must always precede [the formation of the whole]. (294)
How could one who hears only the word "Devadatta" superimpose upon that limited word the entirety of the preceding sentences? (295)
And how is there the comprehension of that much meaning from the sentence?
If you say it is "from that very [sentence]," then in that case, there would be neither hearing of individual words nor [comprehension] thereof. (296)
To that extent, he possesses that object within the scope of primordial nature;
thus, through the complete knowledge of the entire meaning of the Śiva scriptures, which is of a perfect form, [he attains this]. (297)

If one should thus conceive of the Yoga, Sāṃkhya, Ārhata, Nyāya, Pāñcarātra, Śruti, and Smṛti as being entirely complete within the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), [then one has truly understood]. ||298||
Let it be so for now, but it has been discussed that it is not so extensive there;
and the cognition of the Śiva-principle is preceded by its latent impression (saṃskāra). 299.
Otherwise, there would be a transgression for both the instructor and the instructed.
If, however, there were an apprehension of that mental impression (*saṃskāra*), then such would indeed be the purpose of the scripture. (300)
But his Vaiṣṇavism, Sāṃkhya-ness, or even his Śrauta-ness does not persist;
rather, having adopted successive higher refinements from others, he continues to practice them.
In that case, his transgression would be even greater than that of a Vaiṣṇava and others.
But surely, what kind of primary conceptualization could there be regarding this state of non-duality? (302)
"What do you say? You yourself have your functioning impaired by [the notion of] difference;
this very thing is the ultimate duality, for you yourself have resorted to it. (303)
Since I am a Vaiṣṇava seeking spiritual perfection, why should I not possess authority within the Śaiva tradition?
It is you who are yourself deluded by duality, and that due to the force of destiny regarding distinctions.
Therefore, it has been established that there would be a transgression for them [if they were not to worship];
moreover, the deity is worshipped through the yoga of identity (*tādātmya*). ||305||
Having attained identity with Viṣṇu, how could one worship Rudra? Furthermore, it is sung in the Gītā: "Whoever is what, he is indeed that. (306)
The yogas consist of the meditation on identity, and the mantras are one's own [nature]; therefore, when their essence has been meditated upon, they bestow success to one who desires the fruit. (307)
Even for one who desires liberation and seeks it through that scripture, being overcome by the contemplation of its defects is sufficient for such a purpose. (308)
This is, first of all, the primary method: that which is established in a particular [substratum] and has attained a state of identity with it eternally is what is authorized therein. (309)
For this very reason, it is designated as "the cognition to be grasped from that," for it has attained identity [with the object] through the sequence of the procedure for its cultivation. (310)
At that very time, how could a disciple, while grasping a treatise according to its sequential order of earlier and later parts,
join it together by his own intellect, even if it were already composed as a continuous whole? (311)
But he who strives to unite [the self with the Absolute] is the Supreme Lord in person. What could a teacher possibly do for him? He is called a teacher only for others. ||312||
For this very reason, they consider that [the knowledge] comes from none other than those who know the Vedas;
therefore, one who has attained identity with that [knowledge] is designated as a "guru. ||313||
And that [attainment] occurs exactly where and to whatever extent it is [possible], and not otherwise.
But surely, at that time, the meaning of the Vaiṣṇava scriptures consists in the contemplation of Śiva. (314)
Alas, this person of full intelligence prattles on about identity and weightiness;
for in the dramas of Rāma and Rāvaṇa, these are not merely the roles of actors. (315)

By means of the transformation of the costume and so forth, he attains (or, according to another reading, "proceeds") to a state of otherness, reflecting: "I am Viṣṇu himself," or "I am His servant. (316)
"Now I am not thus"—how can this be entirely consistent?
For in this case, one of the two cognitions must be false knowledge. (317)
By this [or "in this manner," as the reading *yathā* suggests], that very disciple would become fallen, or the disciple might fall;
therefore, this primary ritual procedure is indeed the most venerable teacher in every scripture. (318)

It is stated in the independent scriptures (svatantra-śāstra) that he who is devoted to another scripture, or even devoted to that [other] scripture, does not bestow the fruit of accomplishment (siddhi). (319)
In the world as well, there are such traditions regarding the luminaries and other fields:
the Bhāgavatas of Viṣṇu, the Magas of the Sun, those with matted hair and smeared with ashes of Śambhu, the Brāhmaṇas who know the circle of the Mothers, and likewise those of Brahmā.
The Śākyas [should perform rites] for one who has the body of a Buddha for the benefit of sentient beings; likewise, the Arhats for those who are naked;
and whatever deity is worshipped by whom according to their own ritual, for that deity the rite must be performed by them.
Therefore, even if one possessing superior knowledge should be present in that place, he would not be a fit recipient for the authority. ||321||

But for that child who is established in this perfect enlightenment, the teaching of reality, in order to achieve progressively higher levels of realization, [the teacher employs] the instruments of the mind. (322)
Or, for the sake of the perfection of the fruit,
he who possesses the rays of his own being would indeed bestow grace, because of his fullness and his upward-turning activity.
Indeed, in non-duality, what could be "higher"? Nothing at all, for you are deluded by duality; your state is "lower" because duality itself is the lower. (324)

Therefore, whatever others there may be who abide by the injunctions for animal sacrifice—be they Vaiṣṇavas, Buddhists, followers of the Vedas, or proponents of the Upaniṣads (Śrutyanta)—[they are all included]. ||325||
Such individuals as these are never eligible for the Lord’s teaching;
this has been stated elsewhere in the scriptures as well, in the analysis of those who possess the qualification [for practice]. (326)
If a foolish-minded Vaiṣṇava should give a Śaiva mantra to a child, the child, recognizing him as a sinful deceiver, should act rightly toward him. (327)
It has been stated here as well that one who possesses well-practiced knowledge shall be a giver of liberation;
for when supreme knowledge is practiced, there is simply no falling away from it. (328)
Indeed, there is no falling away from supreme non-dual consciousness; its activity is filled with the entirety of knowledge established within the domain of one's own self. (329)
"How," "who," "from where," or even "where" those who pass away might remain—this very meaning of the treatise is established through the power of [the Lord's] capacity. (330)
Filled with the full weight of all the phonemes and principles contained within,
this very Bhairava-nature, which is the designation of all things, possesses its own essential form.
In this treatise, it was composed by the Supreme Lord under the name Jñānacandra.
Thus, this profound yet lucid discourse has been explained by me, following the sequence of establishing the authority of our own tradition and through various incidental digressions.
For those whose intellects have ascended to this [level], the majesty of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is liberated from the bonds of the universe’s duality.
Those whose hearts are truth itself will know that it shines by its own nature; what is the use of praises?
Are those who investigate correctly not indeed auspicious—what effort can be directed against them? What use are those who are like the lame on the path of ascending the peak of profound reflection?
As for these men who are barren of scripture, their very conduct has become like stone.
Then this agitation whirls within itself like the ocean at the time of universal dissolution.
O Fire of the End of the Aeon, be pacified within yourself and quickly abandon the ostentation of your flaming tresses, for there is as yet nothing remaining for you to consume;
by the hundreds of fierce sparks from your flickering, whirling, and thickly crackling flames, [the world has already been reduced to ash].
Having pervaded the universe, this world, which is of the nature of Your radiance, has swiftly returned to a state of dissolution.
In the city named Pravarapura, the Kashmiri Abhinavagupta composed this Vārttika on the Mālinīvijaya and other texts. (335)
Thus ends the second section of the *Śrīmālinīvijayottaraślokavārtika*, composed by the venerable Abhinavagupta, the most excellent teacher of the Great Mahāmaheśvara tradition.
May it be for the sake of auspiciousness.
